entry.title: Cisco gives engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite legacy code
entry.content:
Gen Z can’t catch a break. Entry-level jobs are vanishing; some 40% of bosses say they plan to hire fewer grads because AI can do the job cheaper, and young workers are routinely slammed for showing up late and refusing to put in overtime for free. Cisco’s president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel isn’t buying it—he’s just handed one of the company’s biggest jobs to a 27-year-old he found hidden in the org chart “five levels” below him.

“I’ve given him unlimited tokens because he’s going to refactor code,” Patel told Fortune at a small roundtable dinner. “So I’m like, you can go, you can go nuts.”

The “him” is Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, or “Paddy,” as Patel affectionately calls him. He joined Cisco in 2025 after the $429 billion tech giant acquired EzDubs, the real-time translation startup Krishnamurthy cofounded in 2023. And despite coming in as a former founder with CEO experience, he was, in Patel’s words, “buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic.”

That changed when Patel dropped into Cisco’s San Francisco office, and the pair got talking. Krishnamurthy reckoned he could rewrite Cisco’s legacy code with a two-person team. Patel says even the most AI-forward people on his own team weren’t thinking that way.

So he has given himself four weeks to prove it, with the final goal of refactoring 98% of Cisco’s legacy code within 24 months.

Now, he’s on the hunt for more Paddys: young hires who will “challenge the system and the status quo,” or, as he puts it, be “an energizer bunny that just goes out and kind of revs everyone up.”

Cisco’s president says Gen Z should be teaching his veterans, not doing data entry—and he’s fine with the tension that causes

At most companies, only someone with decades of experience under their belt would be trusted with a project this size. Patel thinks that’s a problem.

“If you don’t hire the early-in-career [workers], and you just let your workforce continue the way that they were, where do fresh ideas get injected? How do you challenge the status quo?” he said.

Seasoned staff can still come up with new ideas, Patel added. What they can’t do is ask the questions that only someone with no experience would think to ask.

And getting the two to get along isn’t always smooth. Patel admits that putting a Gen Zer in a room with people who’ve been at Cisco for decades can create friction—but he says that’s the point.

“Tension is good,” he said. “I actually try to create tension in the teams because you want to have enough friction on the ideas. You don’t want to have friction with people and personalities.”

“What you have to do is establish enough trust with people to say you are going to be expected to create unreasonable goals for yourself,” he added. “And so, in order to go out and achieve those unreasonable goals, think outside of the box.”

And he’s not just pushing senior staff to take notes from twentysomethings. He said that he treats every intern as “kind of a reverse mentor,” and even does talks at colleges to find students who are “hungry.”

His latest Gen Z bet came out of one of those talks, to 17- and 18-year-old Stanford scholarship students. While a line of students fired questions at him, one, Baya, stood off to the side, just listening. She waited until everyone else had finished before she opened up.

He told her to email him every month with what she’d learned about AI. It was a test of follow-through: “Everyone can go out and have one good conversation. But are they going to stick with their commitments?”

She never missed one, landed an internship at Cisco, and redesigned “something” that experienced staff hadn’t been able to crack.

“I didn’t bring her in so that she can do grunt work and do data entry,” he said. “We brought her in so that she could actually teach our people how to think completely differently.” Now he wants to recruit her.

Patel isn’t the only one betting on Gen Z—OpenAI investor Josh Kushner and Will.i.am are hunting for young, hungry talent

Patel isn’t the only boss who sees Gen Z’s lack of experience as an asset.

Thrive Capital’s founder Josh Kushner told Fortune he specifically likes to hire people with less than four years of industry experience.

When he launched the venture capital firm at just 26, he faced pressure to bring in older, more seasoned hires. But, as he put it, “anyone who has experience that is talented will never want to work with a 26-year-old.” So, instead, he recruited the “smartest people that we knew who were our ages.”

And that bet paid off: His firm made early investments in startups worth billions, including OpenAI, which is currently raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation.

These days, Kushner could easily hire industry veterans with glowing résumés—but he’d still rather “find that young, hungry person.”

Alon Chen, founder and CEO of Tastewise—a generative AI platform trusted by PepsiCo, Nestlé, and Mars—is also actively looking for Gen Zers with zero experience.

“I’m hiring entry-level because they have no boundaries or limitations in how they think about the world,” Chen told Fortune. “They’re almost like AI natives themselves, having been born and raised in this new realm of opportunities. And I see some of the best ideas coming from the younger generation that have not yet been in the job market.”

And Will.i.am has reached a similar conclusion. The Grammy-winning Black Eyed Peas frontman might be best known for his chart-topping hits, but behind the scenes, he’s a serious investor too. He backed Tesla, OpenAI, and Pinterest before they became household names—and now, he’s betting on Gen Z for his next investment.

Why? He believes the next big tech breakthroughs will come from young innovators at MIT and Stanford. “They’re young kids, and they’re native to this,” Will.i.am told Fortune. “So you want to hunt for that. That’s the only thing I’m focused on.”

And Patel told Fortune that the trend toward hiring Gen Z will only continue, thanks to AI.

“The only way for us to keep accelerating is to make sure we’re surrounded by people with a broad range of experience,” he said. “Roughly one-third of my team is experienced, scaled operators who understand how the Cisco engine works. The second third are systems thinkers from the market who bring the outside-in perspective. And the final third is made of entrepreneurial founders, CEOs, and engineers who are AI-native who operate in founder mode.”

“Either of these groups by themselves aren’t nearly as potent as when all three work together. It’s what creates magic.”

entry.title: Florilegium: Procedural Flowers in LaTeX
entry.content:
The Reddit post asked how to make flowers like these in LaTeX. I don't know how the original was made. This project is one possible way, and the way I did it uses hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua and placed by a procedural layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature. It gets a similar look, but I explicitly tried to not replicate the original.

This project was made with the assistance of AI (Claude), and I'm sharing the process I used to bring it to life.

Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LaTeX. No images, no imported paths, no external assets: every petal, leaf and stem is a parametric curve computed in Lua while the page is being written, painted like a watercolor, and written straight into the PDF. Every page gets its own garden.

Try it in your browser. The playground sets a page as a printer's proof, grows its margin with the same Lua, and hands it back as an SVG, a LaTeX preamble or a Typst page setup.

Six seeds of the grown composition. Same code, different seed — and the garden fills whatever space the text leaves free.

Two documents share one package, and two more (showcase.tex, spread.tex) show what else it does:

florilegium.tex florilegium-grow.tex composition authored: stems, leaves and flowers placed by hand, every parameter sampled grown: a plant grown to fit the page by a greedy space-filling loop adapts to nothing (tuned for A4, 68 mm margin) the page layout, and the free space below the text on the last page preview

Both PDFs are self-describing: the body text is the write-up of how the margin is drawn.

Last page of the grown document: the text ends early, so branches arch into the space below.

300 dpi crop. Mottled washes with white streaks lifted out, lobed leaves with white veins, forget-me-not cymes, a pale ghost flower behind the stems.

as it grows with the free space it fills

Seed 6, from an empty margin to the finished page. The stems rise first, leaves open as the tips pass their nodes, and each stem ends in a flower. Then the greedy loop takes over: on the right, each dashed circle is the largest free disc it found, just before a branch grows to it. Big holes come first and slowly, small ones last and fast. The butterflies and bees fly in, the bird glides onto its twig, and the snail crawls up its stem until the last frame, which is exactly the page this seed always gives.

The growth is recorded once, while the page is laid out: each stem is also drawn as prefixes of increasing length and each motif at a few smaller scales, replaying the same random draws. A frame then writes the pieces whose time has come, in their original painting order. make grow-6 renders one seed this way (build/grow-6.gif and .mp4, about 45 seconds); add EXPLAIN=1 for the dashed circles.

showcase.tex, "A year in the margin": spring on the first page, summer, autumn on the last. Each section describes the feature it shows.

The grown margin can respond to the document around it:

Initials. \florilegiuminitial[5]{E} sets the first letter of a paragraph in a tile five lines tall. The outline of the letter is read from an OpenType font (Latin Modern Bold by default) and painted like a petal; a vine passes over and under its strokes in turn, with leaves where they fit and flowers in the gaps, often in the letter's counters. The letter is also typeset invisibly, so the paragraph still copies as "Every". Flowers at the headings. With the option sections, every numbered section and subsection gets a flower in the margin beside its heading, painted in the copper of the accents, the way headings were once picked out in red. A flower where the text asks. \florilegiumbloom puts a flower beside the line it stands in; \florilegiumbloom[lily] asks for any motif of the garden. The marks are found in the page box when the page is shipped out, so this works in one run. Seasons. With the option aging, the garden ages from spring on the first page (mostly in bud, small pale leaves) to autumn on the last (seed heads, falling petals, a few copper leaves). It needs two runs, for the page count; \florilegiumage{0.8} sets an age by hand instead.

One seed in spring, early summer, late summer and autumn. The seasons change what grows, not where.

Most pages have visitors: a butterfly or two and bees in the open spaces, a snail crawling up one of the main stems, and on about one page in five a bird perched on a twig of its own. They come from a random stream of their own, so a page without them is exactly the page it would have been; the option novisitors leaves them out.

The whole palette comes from one color, ink: Delft blue, sepia, green, crimson, violet, teal. The ramp from the darkest stroke to the palest wash is computed from that hue in OKLCH, so the light end never turns gray.

Seed 6 three times: as it always grew, with theme=geometric, and with theme=math.

The growth loop never knew what it was drawing. It reads a table of motifs (the size of the disc each one takes, a weight, a function that draws it) and calls every primitive by name. A theme is one Lua file, theme-<name>.lua, that replaces some of those primitives and may add rows to the table, or brings a composition of its own.

theme=geometric is the same plant cut from flat shapes (theme-geometric.lua). It grows exactly as the flowers do, and only the drawing changes: the stems run straight between their nodes, the leaves are kites and toothed polygons folded into a light and a dark facet with straight white veins, the flowers are rosettes of rhombi or layered star polygons, the tendrils square spirals, the bird and the butterfly low-poly. The colors are flat tones of the ink, with no wash; crystals (Platonic solids, flat-shaded like cut stones) grow among the flowers. A page is about a tenth of the size of a flora page.

theme=math is no plant at all (theme-math.lua, drawing from figures.lua): mathematics cascading down the margin and across the bottom of the page, overlapping a little so it blends. A large figure sits in the corner where the column meets the bottom (an Apollonian gasket, a deep Koch snowflake, Vogel's disc, a polyhedron). Down the column run one or two families, figures that change as they go, joined by small copper arrows: the Koch snowflake gaining a level, a polygon gaining sides on its way to the circle, the cube truncating into the octahedron, chords k → mk mod n turning from a cardioid into a nephroid, Vogel's disc packing evenly only at the golden angle. Equations that hold (e^{iπ} + 1 = 0, V − E + F = 2, ...) run along the bottom and under the text on the last page, and everything else, largest hole first, is figures (Platonic solids, knots, Hilbert curves, Lissajous curves, hypotrochoids, Maurer roses, the Petersen graph, ...), letters, numerals and symbols set by TeX at many sizes and a slight tilt, and dots. It fills whatever space the page leaves, like the garden; density sets how much there is.

\usepackage[grown,theme=geometric]{florilegium} % or theme=math; the whole document \florilegiumtheme{math} % or from the page this stands on

A document without a theme comes out byte for byte as it did before themes existed.

Seed 6 at density=1, 0.5, 0.2 and 0.05, and at intensity=0.5.

A full garden is a lot to have beside an equation. Two options turn it down, with any theme:

density=0.4 grows less: the loop stops at larger holes, keeps more paper around each motif, and hangs fewer leaves and fillers. Low on the dial the plant itself thins out: two main stems, then one, no footer; at 0.05 it is a single vine with its flower, a couple of leaves and one or two sprays. With the math theme it means fewer things. intensity=0.5 paints the whole margin paler, the same way the ghost flowers behind the garden are painted. It changes only the color, not the detail. \usepackage[grown,density=0.4,intensity=0.6]{florilegium}

At the defaults (1 and 1) every page is exactly the page it was before.

Or no margin at all: \florilegiumornament{leaf} sets one primitive in the line, in a box the size of a letter, for example to open a paragraph. Each ornament in a document gets a shape of its own and keeps it from one build to the next; seed=random draws a new one every time the PDF is built, and seed=7 a fixed one.

\usepackage[nomargin]{florilegium} % ornaments only, no garden in the margin \florilegiumornament{leaf} A paragraph that opens with a leaf. \florilegiumornament[size=2.4em, ink=5B2A1F, angle=30, seed=random]{flower}

Any primitive works (leaf, leaflet, flower, blossom, bud, bell, lily, cyme, umbel, butterfly, bee, bird, hedera, sparkle, ...), and so do the current theme's (crystal with geometric; knot, polyhedron, koch, ... with math).

spread.tex, pages 2 and 3: a two-sided document with a wide outer margin. The garden grows on the left of the left-hand page and, mirrored, on the right of the right-hand page. The last page also switches to the geometric theme.

The garden grows in whichever side margin is wider, so there is nothing to set. In a two-sided document (twoside with a wide outer margin) it changes sides with the page. A one-sided document with a wide right margin gets it on the right of every page. A mirrored page is laid out as if seen in a mirror, then drawn through a reflection: the last transform that every point already passes through. It is exactly the reflection of the garden the same seed would grow on the left.

The playground, seed 12 in autumn on a last page. The page is a proof, and its colophon, the note a book keeps about its paper, ink and printing, is the set of controls: every copper word in it can be changed.

The same Lua can draw a page without TeX. svg.lua runs the package's own code with a small stand-in for the few parts of TeX it touches (the page's lengths, the page number, and the node a drawing goes into), takes the PDF drawing commands that ink.lua writes as it always does, and rewrites them as SVG. Nothing in the drawing code changes, so the garden is the one LuaLaTeX would draw, not an imitation of it.

texlua svg.lua --seed 7 > margin.svg # page 1 of a document with \def\florilegiumseed{7} lua svg.lua --seed 7 --season autumn --ink 5B2A1F --left 25mm --right 65mm > margin.svg texlua svg.lua --help # paper, margins, two-sided pages, the last page, themes... make svg SEED=7 # -> build/svg-7.svg

Any Lua 5.3 or 5.4 runs it. Lengths are read the way TeX reads them and colors are converted the way xcolor converts them, so --seed 7 with the default margins gives, byte for byte, the drawing on page 1 of florilegium-grow.tex built with seed 7. The SVG is a whole page with a transparent background, which makes it a page background anywhere. In Typst:

#set page(paper: "a4", margin: (left: 68mm, right: 22mm, top: 32mm, bottom: 30mm), background: image("margin.svg", width: 100%, height: 100%))

The playground runs the same files in the browser with wasmoon, Lua 5.4 compiled to WebAssembly, in a background worker, and a page grows in about a second. Seed 7 there is seed 7 here. The proof is the control surface as much as the colophon is: the measure above it sets the margin, and dragging the foot of the text up makes a last page. The text on the proof describes the garden that just grew, from the counts the growth loop keeps. Under it, the page can be seen as readers with protanopia, deuteranopia or tritanopia see it, with the distance between the ink and the accent measured for each (Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes's model, distances in Oklab); a pairing that is hard to tell apart is flagged when you choose it. Next to the download are the LaTeX preamble, the Typst setup and the command line that make the same garden, and the address bar keeps every setting, so a garden can be shared as a link.

To run it from a clone, serve the repository with make playground and open http://localhost:8000/web/. The math theme works too. Its figures come from the same Lua; its equations and symbols, which TeX sets in a PDF, are set in the playground by MathJax in the same Computer Modern, and the command line leaves them out. The fonts are served with the page (IM FELL DW Pica, and Latin Modern renamed as its license asks), so nothing is fetched from a font service.

postscript/florilegium.ps: the grown margin in pure PostScript, one self-contained file. Ghostscript, or a printer, computes every petal while it interprets the page, and the two pages of text explain how.

The drawing core, every primitive and the growth loop are ported from ink.lua, flora.lua and grow.lua, procedure for procedure. It needs no TeX and no other file:

gs -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dSeed=7 -o garden.pdf postscript/florilegium.ps make postscript # the same -> build/postscript-7.pdf; SEED=12 for another garden

-dSeed=N picks the garden; without it the clock picks one, so every print is new. -dAge=0 to 1 sets the season, and -dNoVisitors leaves out the butterflies, bees, snail and bird. Two pages take about 2.5 seconds. Much of the Lua maps directly: PostScript's own transformation matrix places each primitive (translate, rotate, scale), paths and Bézier curves are native, and procedures built at run time stand in for Lua's closures (a petal's half-width is a procedure handed to the outline builder). Four things don't map:

Layers. The garden grows in one order but is painted back to front, so every fill and stroke is captured with pathforall into a list per layer, and the lists are played back at the end. Transparency. PostScript has none. Ghostscript provides it with -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY. Without that flag, or on a printer, each translucent fill is mixed with the color it is likely to land on and painted opaque. The result is flatter, but it's the same garden. Randomness. The generator is Park-Miller in 32-bit integer arithmetic, and PostScript reals are single precision, so seed 7 here is a different garden from seed 7 in LaTeX. Text. The file typesets its own two pages in Times. It knows where its headings are and where its text ends, so the copper flowers at the headings and the garden under the last line work as they do in LaTeX. It has no initials, animation, themes, mirrored pages, density or intensity, ornaments in the text, or authored composition.

The file sent twice to an Epson inkjet with lp postscript/florilegium.ps, with no seed given. The computer's print system runs the program again for each job, so each print takes its seed from the clock and grows a different garden. A printer gets the opaque version, as it has no transparency.

LuaLaTeX, one pass, about a second a page (two passes for showcase.tex, whose seasons need the page count).

make # the four PDFs make seed-7 # one page from seed 7 -> build/seed-7.pdf make gallery # gallery/seeds.png + seeds.gif, inks.png, seasons.png, themes.png, dials.png (python3, Pillow, pdftoppm) make grow-6 # growth animation of seed 6 -> build/grow-6.gif + .mp4 (ffmpeg) make grow-6 EXPLAIN=1 # the same with the free discs marked -> build/grow-6-explain.* make svg SEED=7 # the same page as SVG, without TeX -> build/svg-7.svg make playground # the browser playground at http://localhost:8000/web/

No TeX installed? Build the image once and run everything in it:

docker build -t florilegium-tex tools make RUN=tools/in-docker

Or paste florilegium.sty, the .lua files and one of the .tex files into an Overleaf project and set the compiler to LuaLaTeX.

Use it in your own document:

\usepackage[grown]{florilegium} % or plain \usepackage{florilegium} for the authored one % options for the grown one: sections (flowers at the headings), aging (two runs), % novisitors (no butterflies, bees, snails or birds); for both: theme=geometric or theme=math, % density=0.4 (grown only), intensity=0.6 % two-sided? nothing to set: the garden grows in the wider side margin \definecolor{ink}{HTML}{5B2A1F} % optional: the hue of the whole palette (this is sepia) \definecolor{accent}{HTML}{B4662F} % optional: the copper of the hairlines ... \florilegiuminitial[4]{T}his paragraph starts with a decorated T. ... a flower in the margin beside this line\florilegiumbloom ... \florilegiumage{0.8} % grown only: autumn from here on \florilegiumtheme{geometric} % another theme, from the page this stands on \florilegiumornament{leaf} % one leaf in the text, the size of a letter \florilegiumtextend % grown only: at the very end of the text

A fixed seed instead of the page number: lualatex "\def\florilegiumseed{7}\input{florilegium-grow.tex}".

Any primitive can be drawn on its own inside a TikZ picture, under the current scope's shift, rotation and scale:

\begin{tikzpicture} \begin{scope}[shift={(2,2)},rotate=20]\florilegiumdraw{flower}{1.3}\end{scope} \begin{scope}[shift={(5,0)}]\florilegiumdraw{leaf}{3.0, {depth=0.6}}\end{scope} \begin{scope}[shift={(8,1)}]\florilegiumdraw{ghost}{"lily", {s=1.4}}\end{scope} \begin{scope}[shift={(11,1)}]\florilegiumdraw{butterfly}{1.5}\end{scope} \end{tikzpicture}

With a theme, its primitives can be drawn by name too: \florilegiumdraw{crystal}{1.0} under theme=geometric (see specimen-geometric.tex), \florilegiumdraw{knot}{1.2} under theme=math.

Drawing (ink.lua). All geometry is computed in Lua and written as PDF path operators into one literal node per page; TeX does no arithmetic. Primitives are drawn in a local frame under an affine transform, which is read from TikZ when a primitive is called inside a scope. Colors come from a tone ramp derived from the one document color ink: navy to mist at the hue of ink, interpolated in OKLCH so the light end stays blue instead of turning gray. Tapered strokes are two offset Béziers, not sampled ribbons.

Primitives (flora.lua). Painted in the order a watercolorist would: a flat wash, darker blotches multiplied over it, pigment pooling at the edges, streaks lifted out in white, a few fine veins, and almost no outlines. Broad petals and flowers, star lilies seen at a tilt, blossoms and florets, buds and bellflowers; lobed and entire leaves; forget-me-not cymes that curl like a scorpion's tail, branching sprigs, umbels, tendrils, seed heads; butterflies, bees, snails and a bird; copper sparkles, rosettes and the ivy-leaf fleuron whose stem becomes the head rule. Any of them can be painted as a pale ghost.

Authored composition (authored.lua). A plant grows from a root in the bottom-left corner: three stems through hand-picked control points, a fourth along the bottom of the page as the footer, leaves at chosen fractions of the stems, and every other motif on a branch that leaves its stem tangentially and arrives along the motif's axis — so every flower can be traced back to the root.

Grown composition (grow.lua), in the spirit of Wong, Zongker & Salesin, Computer-Generated Floral Ornament (SIGGRAPH 1998). The stems sway up the column as smooth noise of their height; leaves are hung at their nodes where there is room. Then, repeatedly: take the largest free disc within reach of a stem, choose a motif that fits it, and grow a branch to it from the nearest stem point; the branch becomes a stem in turn. Big holes are taken first, so flowers and lilies land early, sprays and leaves fill the middle, and the loop ends by tucking leaflets, buds and florets onto the stems. The end of the text is measured with \pagetotal in the same pass, so a short last page grows branches into the space below it with one compilation.

Reading the page (florilegium.lua). A heading or \florilegiumbloom leaves an invisible marker node in the text. When the page is shipped out, its box is walked node by node, adding up heights, depths and the glue as it was set, to find each marker's height on the page; the garden then gives those lines their flowers before any leaf is hung. An age reweights the motifs: buds and sprays of buds in spring, seed heads in autumn, when some leaves are painted with a ramp built from the accent instead of the ink.

Initials (initial.lua). The letter's outline comes from luaotfload's OpenType reader as Bézier segments. Flattened into polygons, it gives an even-odd inside test, and a grid of distances to the letter and the frame finds the largest gaps for the flowers. The vine is a Catmull-Rom curve across the tile; where it crosses the letter it goes over and under in turn, and the strands that go over are drawn again, clipped to the letter, with a thin halo of paper.

Procedural ≠ random. The seed is derived from the page number, so page n always gets garden n. Reproducibility is what makes the document stable enough to typeset.

See CLAUDE.md for a handoff-style map of the code, the tunables, and ideas not yet done.

The Reddit post that asked the question (see Origin). The growth loop follows Wong, Zongker & Salesin, Computer-Generated Floral Ornament (SIGGRAPH 1998). The tone ramp is computed in Oklab, Björn Ottosson's perceptual color space; the conversion matrices in ink.lua are his, released into the public domain. The random numbers come from mulberry32, Tommy Ettinger's public-domain generator. \florilegiumornament, its ink and seed=random keys, and the density option answer issue #4 from rubyFeedback. The playground runs the Lua in the browser with wasmoon (MIT) and typesets the math theme's equations with MathJax (Apache 2.0), both loaded from jsDelivr. It is set in Igino Marini's IM FELL DW Pica (SIL OFL) and Latin Modern (GUST e-foundry, GUST Font License); see web/fonts/README.md. Its color-blindness views use the model of Machado, Oliveira & Fernandes, A Physiologically-based Model for Simulation of Color Vision Deficiency (IEEE TVCG, 2009). The math theme's figures keep the names of the people they come from: Maurer's roses, Vogel's model of the sunflower, Temple Fay's butterfly curve, the Petersen graph, Koch's snowflake, Hilbert's curve, Lissajous figures, the gasket of Apollonius.

entry.title: Show HN: A working Nintendo in ~1GB of Qwen weights

An NES CPU compiled into the weights of a stock Qwen3.5 model.

The NES's 6502 CPU (the core of its 2A03 chip), its 2 KB of work RAM, and a cartridge's program ROM run inside a standard Qwen3_5ForCausalLM checkpoint. Nobody trained these weights; a compiler computed every one. When you play a game, the model predicts the CPU's execution log one token at a time. A small host program plays the rest of the console around it: it draws the picture, reads the controller, and fires the vblank interrupt.

nesformer builds on Qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, which compiled a CHIP-8 and then a RISC-V CPU into Qwen3.5-4B. It reuses Qwenputer's compiler and its central trick: the model's Gated DeltaNet state is the machine's memory.

Super Mario Bros. (World 1-1) Full Game by Doug Fraker (title screen and first level)

Every CPU token in these runs came from the model. For the bundled test games, every frame also matches a conventional 6502 emulator's output exactly (see How it was checked).

Unzip nesformer.zip and nesformer-weights.zip into the same folder. The weights go next to the nesformer/ package, not inside it:

nesformer/ <- run commands from here ├── nesformer/ <- the Python package ├── chipformer/ <- Qwenputer's compiler ├── roms/ <- test ROMs (put your own here too) ├── examples/ <- sample GIFs and frame sheets ├── tests/ ├── LICENSE ├── LICENSE.chipformer ├── README.md ├── pyproject.toml └── weights/ <- from nesformer-weights.zip ├── config.json ├── generation_config.json ├── model.safetensors ├── nesformer.json └── SHA256SUMS

The CLI looks for weights/ beside the nesformer/ package. To keep the weights elsewhere, pass --weights /path/to/weights to run, check or trace, or give the path to info.

To confirm the weights unzipped correctly, run shasum -a 256 -c weights/SHA256SUMS from the top folder.

You need Python 3.11 or newer.

python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install numpy scipy numba pillow python -m nesformer run roms/thwaite.nes --frames 600 --show \ --buttons "start@90-95+200-205,a@230-233+250-253+270-273+290-293+310-313+330-333+350-353+370-373+390-393+410-413+430-433+450-453+470-473+490-493+510-513+530-533+550-553+570-573+590-593"

--show draws each frame in your terminal as the model generates it. When the run ends, the CLI saves an animated GIF named after the ROM (here thwaite.gif) in the current folder.

Expect it to be slow. The first run spends about 20 seconds compiling the engine with numba. After that, a frame takes 1–6 seconds, so 600 frames (10 seconds of NES time) take around 25 minutes.

Point run at any .nes file that uses the NROM board (iNES mapper 0), such as Super Mario Bros., Donkey Kong or Excitebike. You supply the ROM; nesformer only ships the three freely licensed test ROMs in roms/.

python -m nesformer run roms/smb.nes --frames 600 --show \ --buttons "start@60-65,right@200-600,a@250-265+300-315+360-375+420-435+480-495+540-555"

That script starts the game, then walks Mario right and jumps about once a second. The CLI loads the ROM into the model's state at startup, so the same weights run any NROM game without a rebuild. Games on other boards stop with a message: see Limitations.

--buttons takes a comma-separated list of entries. Each entry names one or more buttons joined by +, then @, then one or more frame ranges joined by +:

start@60-65 press Start during frames 60 to 65 right@200-600 hold Right from frame 200 to frame 600 a@250-265+300-315 press A twice right+b@200-600 hold Right and B together (run, in Super Mario Bros.)

The buttons are a, b, select, start, up, down, left and right. Frames count from power-on at 60 per second, so frame 600 is 10 seconds in. Games ignore input on screens where you can't move, so holding a button a little early does no harm. In Super Mario Bros., a longer A press makes a higher jump.

Command What it does python -m nesformer run ROM Play a ROM on the weights and save a GIF python -m nesformer check ROM Run the weights and the reference CPU side by side; stop at the first difference python -m nesformer trace ROM Print the model's token stream (default 40 tokens) python -m nesformer build Compile the circuit and write weights/ (about 10 seconds) python -m nesformer info Describe the checkpoint

Options for run:

Option Default Meaning --frames N 120 Stop after N frames --buttons SCRIPT none Controller input (see above) --show off Draw frames in the terminal (needs 24-bit color, e.g. iTerm2 or Windows Terminal) --gif PATH ROM name Where to save the animated GIF --png DIR off Save each kept frame as a PNG in DIR. With --png alone, no GIF is saved. Add --gif to get both. --every N 1 Keep every N-th frame --scale N 2 Enlarge saved frames N times --engine fast fast (numba), numpy, or hf (stock transformers; needs torch, ~10 tokens/s) --no-skip off Run every iteration of idle wait loops (slower; identical frames) --max-tokens N none Stop after N tokens --trace FILE none Save the token ids

run, check and trace all accept --weights, --engine, --buttons and --no-skip. check --tokens N sets how far to compare (default 50,000). trace --tokens N sets how many tokens to print (default 40). build --out DIR writes the checkpoint somewhere other than weights/.

In the model (weights + DeltaNet state) In the host (nesformer/host.py) The 6502 core: all 151 official opcodes, every addressing mode, flags, stack, BRK and NMI entry The PPU: a scanline renderer and the palette 2 KB of work RAM Controllers; APU registers (written, otherwise ignored) 32 KB of PRG-ROM, stored twice: one copy for instruction fetch, one for data reads NMI timing at vblank, injected as an NMI token OAM DMA reads (the 256 bytes appear as DM tokens) Answers to I/O reads, injected as IN tokens

This split follows Qwenputer's CHIP-8 build, whose host injects timer ticks and draws the display from the trace. The host never sees the CPU's registers or RAM except through the trace.

The memory trick works like this. Each DeltaNet head keeps a 128 × 128 state matrix that the delta rule updates at every token. With the gate held open and a one-hot key, an update overwrites exactly one row of that matrix, and a one-hot query reads it back. So every row is a memory cell, and the cartridge, RAM and registers all live in rows.

weights/ is an ordinary Hugging Face folder. It loads with Qwen3_5ForCausalLM.from_pretrained and needs no custom code.

Architecture Qwen3_5ForCausalLM, with Qwen3.5-4B's DeltaNet head shapes (16 key heads, 32 value heads, dim 128) and MLP width (9,216) Layers 7 Gated DeltaNet layers (the circuit), plus 1 all-zero attention layer that Hugging Face's cache needs Hidden size 768 Vocabulary 263,808 tokens Parameters 466.6M in bf16 (933 MB), of which 9.3M are nonzero, so the weights zip to 3.3 MB

nesformer.json records which layer and head holds each part of the machine. A run writes the cartridge, registers and RAM into those DeltaNet states, then decodes greedily.

Layer Attention (state) MLP 1 PC anchor; instruction counters; A, X, Y, SP; flags N V Z C I D; pointer latches; NMI flag counter thermometers; SP ± 1; LO + Y 2 — PC = anchor + bytes executed since; PC + 1, PC + 2 3 PRG fetch: opcode and two operand bytes at the PC opcode decode; operand bits; indexed sums; branch test and target 4 — effective address, by addressing mode and record stage; the byte a push stores 5 RAM and PRG data reads at the effective address operand; ADC/SBC adder, compares, BIT; address decode 6 — result byte, carry, overflow, flags, jump targets 7 — the next token

Each instruction becomes a record, and the record's last token commits it. As in Qwenputer's RISC-V core, the PC is implied rather than written: each final token carries its instruction's length, three DeltaNet counters tally the instructions of each length since the last jump, and the PC is the jump target plus that offset. Excerpts from Full Game:

SEI P(000100 px0 L1) LDX #$40 X($40 c0 v0 px0 L2) STX $4017 IOW($4017=$40 L3) TXS S($FF L1) BIT $2002 IOR($2002) IN($00) P(000110 px0 L3) <- the host injects IN BPL $8017 J($8017) JSR $8279 PSH($FE) PSH($FD) J($8279) <- the return address is pushed in-circuit RTS PUL($FC) LO($7B) PUL($FD) J($827C) STA ($72),Y LO($08) HI($03) ST($00 a7=0 L2) <- pointer bytes latched, then the store STA $4014 IOW($4014=$02 L0) DM(0:$FF) … DM(255:$00) NT(L3) <- OAM DMA

Most instructions take a single token; real game code averages 1.1–1.3 tokens per instruction. nesformer/spec.py documents every token family.

The reference CPU (nesformer/cpu.py) matches nestest's golden log for 3,348 instructions, and the py65 emulator on 5.7 million instructions of game code.

The exact circuit, run in Qwenputer's evaluator with its bf16 exactness checks, predicts every reference token: all of nestest plus 283,610 positions of two games' boot sequences.

The checkpoint in stock transformers (bf16, CPU) predicts 2,651 positions of nestest and Full Game with no mismatches.

The weights, free-running, generate traces identical to the reference CPU's:

Run Tokens Frames NES time Result nestest (official opcodes) 4,586 — — identical, ending in the expected HALT Thwaite, check 700,000 271 4.5 s identical trace and frames Thwaite, run 1,916,527 600 10.0 s all 300 saved frames match Full Game, run 2,645,885 420 7.0 s all 210 saved frames match

The idle-loop skip changes nothing visible: frames and I/O writes, cycle timestamps included, match a run without it.

The default engine computes Qwen3.5's forward pass from model.safetensors, compiled with numba and skipping the all-zero blocks. It ran at about 1,650 tokens/s on one CPU core of the machine it was built on. The plain numpy engine does about 210, and stock transformers about 10. A real NES would need about 700,000 tokens per second.

Games spend most of each frame in a loop that waits for vblank. When the host sees a loop body repeat exactly, with no RAM or I/O writes, it advances the clock to just before the next PPU event, and the remaining iterations still run. That cuts the token count by 2.6× to 4.2×. Overall, nesformer runs 150–290× slower than the real console.

NROM cartridges only (iNES mapper 0). The CPU can address only 32 KB of program ROM at a time. Bigger games carry a bank-switching chip (a mapper, such as MMC1 or MMC3) that swaps which part of the ROM the CPU sees. nesformer's ROM reads happen inside the model, from a fixed 32 KB table, so it can't follow a bank switch yet. Supporting a mapper means storing the whole ROM in the state, keeping the bank registers there too, and adding one stage that turns each CPU address into a ROM address. Official opcodes only. An unofficial opcode emits HALT. Code must run from the cartridge ROM. A jump into RAM emits HALT. No IRQs (APU frame IRQ, DMC). BRK and NMI work. Read-modify-write instructions on I/O registers don't produce an I/O write, and $4020–$7FFF reads as 0 (no PRG-RAM). The PPU and APU aren't in the weights. The PPU renders one scanline at a time, so mid-scanline effects aren't reproduced. Sprite-0 hit and sprite overflow are approximate, and there's no sound. pip install pytest py65 python -m pytest -q tests

The tests take a few minutes. They check the reference CPU against nestest's log, the circuit against the reference, the weights free-running against the reference, and the idle-loop skip.

pip install "torch>=2.6" "transformers>=5.22" python -m nesformer run roms/thwaite.nes --frames 3 --engine hf

nesformer/hfcheck.py shows the whole procedure: load the checkpoint, decode one padding token, write the machine's state into the cache's DeltaNet states, then feed tokens one at a time.

Path Contents nesformer/spec.py token families and records nesformer/cpu.py the reference 6502 that writes the trace nesformer/host.py everything around the CPU: PPU, controllers, NMI timing, cycle counting, idle skip nesformer/core.py the circuit and the state snapshot nesformer/weights.py the emitter that turns the circuit into a Qwen3_5ForCausalLM checkpoint nesformer/engine.py, fastengine.py run the weights (numpy / numba) nesformer/hfcheck.py run the weights in stock transformers nesformer/run.py, check.py, cli.py, __main__.py drivers, the teacher-forced check, the CLI chipformer/ Qwenputer's q35 compiler (q35/ emitter and primitives, dsl/ graph) weights/ the compiled checkpoint and its SHA-256 checksum roms/ test ROMs; roms/SOURCES.md lists their authors and licenses examples/ GIFs and frame sheets from the runs; demo.gif is the Super Mario Bros. run shown at the top tests/test_nesformer.py the test suite
Qwenputer and its chipformer compiler: MIT, © 2026 Divyansh Agrawal (LICENSE.chipformer). That license also covers the code adapted from Qwenputer in nesformer/core.py and nesformer/weights.py. Its last paragraph refers to Qwenputer's CHIP-8 ROMs, which this repository does not include. Test ROMs: nestest by Kevin Horton; Full Game by Doug Fraker (MIT); Thwaite by Damian Yerrick (GPL-3.0, source at pinobatch/thwaite-nes).

entry.title: My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii
The oldest ice disappears and the Stone Age emerges from it
entry.content:
The oldest ice is disappearing: The Stone Age is emerging from the melting ice

'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape,' write the glacial archaeologists. Finds from the Viking Age are becoming scarce, while 6,000-year-old arrowheads are now emerging from the melting ice.

For exactly 20 years, archaeologists working with Secrets of the Ice have been recovering and preserving artefacts emerging from the ice in the mountains of Innlandet, eastern Norway.

Until now, most of the objects have been up to 2,000 years old. Many date from the Viking Age.

But the ancient ice is now beginning to melt.

And within this oldest ice lie the oldest finds: large quantities of arrow shafts and arrowheads from the Bronze Age and the Stone Age.

Here comes the Stone Age

One of the oldest finds from this year's first field expedition is an arrow with an arrowhead and shaft made of slate.

By comparing it with previously discovered arrows, archaeologists estimate that it is between 5,000 and 6,000 years old.

The fact that arrows are emerging from the melting ice is not surprising. Over the 20 years they have been working here, the archaeologists have found extensive evidence of reindeer and reindeer hunting. They have also found clothing, shoes, dead packhorses, and a pair of skis.

The preservation conditions in the ice have meant that organic material, such as wood, leather, and textiles, have also survived.

“This year, we found 48 prehistoric arrows. That's a lot,” Espen Finstad, who leads Secrets of the Ice, tells Science Norway.

He explains that, with these latest discoveries, more than 100 arrowheads and arrow shafts have now been recovered from a single ice patch over the years.

The oldest arrowheads are made from slate, freshwater mussel shells, and bone. More recent arrowheads are made from iron and are 'only' between 1,000 and 1,500 years old.

A brutal backdrop

But this year’s fieldwork carries an added sense of gravity.

Finstad explains that the work of recovering archaeological artefacts from the ice has always carried a certain duality.

“It’s fun going around looking for things. It’s exciting, and finding something is just really cool," he says.

Yet behind the excitement lies the reality of climate change. Finstad points to the recent landslide in Nepal and the glacier collapse in Jotunheimen.

“We have always acknowledged this contradiction and the reality behind our work. But this is the first time it has truly affected us on an emotional level,” Finstad says, adding:

“This year, there was a much deeper sense of seriousness and sadness. Only patches of ice remain where we once had large ice patches. It's brutal. And this year, that reality struck us more forcefully than ever before."

Finstad and his colleagues estimate that most of the ice patches containing archaeological artefacts will have disappeared within the next 20 years.

“There has been ice here for 6,000–7,000 years. Nature has been warning us and sending signals for many years. But now it's giving up. Now it is simply going to melt,” says the glacial archaeologist.

'For thousands of years, ancient ice has safely preserved unique objects from the past. Now that ice is disappearing,' the archaeologists write in a press release about the finds. 'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape.'

More fieldwork ahead

Finstad and his colleagues are planning more fieldwork in the coming weeks, weather permitting.

So far, they have secured finds in the Kvittingskjølen mountain area of Jotunheimen, specifically at Langfonne, Storefonne, and Hanklefonne.

Several of the finds are already on display at the Norwegian Mountain Centre in Lom, just a few days after they were discovered.

Digital minimalism
entry.content:
For a long time I have been a fan of minimalism in my physical life: have few physical possessions, and try to do more with less. Four years ago, I wrote this blog post describing what I had in the 40-liter backpack that I travel around with.

Physical minimalism, however, was an idea that came of age in the 2000s and 2010s and was responding to the challenges and the opportunities of the 2000s and 2010s. I continue to believe that it is valuable - though I recognize some arguments in the other direction, notably that having the right kinds of physical things can make more practical to have more self-sovereignty over your life. But I also think that in the modern era, we need a new kind of minimalism: digital minimalism.

Digital minimalism is about being intentional about ways that you access digital technology, making each use a conscious choice rather than something that you get sucked into by default. In this post, I will describe some experiments that I've done in this direction.

Twitter (aka X) has always had a strain of toxicity to it, that has been increasing in recent years. The platform is definitely engaging, but it's often far from informative, and the ways in which it engages often do not make you feel good. But this all seemed to hit a particular crescendo for me around the end of 2024 and beginning of 2025. Many things were happening at that moment, but if you spent a lot of time on X you will likely remember a particular one: everyone seemed to be suddenly becoming fans of Adolf Hitler.

This is not even mentioning the time that Grok itself briefly turned into "MechaHitler".

Around the same time, "Crypto Twitter" was spiraling into a mood that I saw described as "financial nihilism": roughly, that the natural end state of blockchains is gambling, this is good, and if you dislike this and wish for something better then you are a stuck-up elitist prick.

Naturally, I had (and continue to have) my intellectual disagreements with both of these trends. But on top of that, I also started to more seriously pay attention to the fact that while the style of discourse on the platform was engaging, it was not enlightening and not making me feel good. And so for much of this year, I have been doing an experiment in distancing myself somewhat from this chaos. I did not leave X the platform, but I did leave X the interface. Instead, I have been doing most of my tweeting through Firefly:

Firefly is a multi-client that combines together X, BlueSky as well as Farcaster and Lens (both partially-Ethereum-based decentralized social media platforms). You can see tweets from all four platforms, and you can make a tweet that gets auto-posted to all four platforms.

My primary goal in doing this was to support decentralized social media, and to continue to engage with X but in a way that distributes network effect rather than locking it in. But in my months of using Firefly, I found that it also has a different effect: I feel much better using it.

I suspect the primary reason is that while Firefly allows you to tweet, and see other people's tweets, it is missing one central part of the X interface: The Algorithmâ¢.

In particular, I suspect that in my time using the X interface, I fell into the following trap:

Now, in fairness to X and Elon and its hard-working employees, the Adolf Hitler fandom does seem to have greatly wound down in the one and a half years since then. I suspect part of this is because such movements inevitably burn out once people realize how immoral and stupid they are. But another part is undoubtedly genuine improvements in how The Algorithmâ¢ works.

But even still, in those moments when I go back into the X interface, I find myself logging back out and going back to Firefly. I also find that my mind has changed. I find myself less interested in the various battles that the intellectual titans on the platform seem to be sucking every day of their lives into. Recently, I logged back in, and I learned that the culture war issue du jour was that people were stridently arguing about whether or not Mao was evil. When I saw this, I had an emotional response that was sort of similar to what I think is the common experience of being an adult, seeing some food or TV show or game that you used to love as a kid, and realizing that you now find no interest in it at all. I smiled, and immediately went back to enjoying my day.

My verdict: I recommend more people try this. Explore ways of greatly decreasing or scoping your social media use: use something like Firefly, access X only on Tuesdays, whatever works for you. Get the information benefits of the platform without getting sucked in to the vortex, which does operate on you in powerful subconscious ways that you may not realize.

For a period of 100 days, I embarked upon a second experiment: I lived my life with my phone always on airplane mode. I still used wifi, but not my cell connection.

I had two goals in doing this:

On the whole, I consider the experiment to have been a success. During those 100 days, I violated the "no cell data" rule once literally but not spiritually - I turned it on briefly to receive a confirmation code that I needed in order to maintain that phone plan itself, and once spiritually but not literally - when going on a remote and slightly dangerous hike, friends insisted that I bring along a few communication devices that they had for emergency comms and use them to check in once every few hours.

My largest inconvenience was a stretch of time I was in Singapore, when my inability to receive SMS confirmation codes meant that I could not log into Grab (the regional Uber equivalent). As a result, my food options were more limited, and I had to take the subway instead of a car even in situations where that was much more inconvenient.

Since those 100 days, I have opened the cell connection occasionally, but so far I have broadly continued an "airplane mode by default" lifestyle.

For navigation, I used CoMaps, a local-first mapping application that downloads OpenStreetMap data and then shows you a map, gives you directions to get where you need, etc locally. My general review of CoMaps is that I find it worse than Google Maps for navigating the human world (restaurants, stores, opening hours...) but better for navigating the natural-ish world (it knows about many trails that Google Maps does not, though it does occasionally fail by claiming trails that do not actually exist, leaving me on one occasion pushing through hundreds of meters of shrubbery to get back to civilization).

I also became interested in the concept of local world knowledge apps. In principle, the data size of meaningful packs of information about the whole world is not that large. Compressed English wikipedia (without media) is only 27 GB. OpenStreetMap's planet.asm is 2.2 TB, though you can doubtlessly prune that down to 1-10% of its size and have everything you might conceivably need.

This month there was a bounty (organized by Statuette; I contributed as one of the donors) to create local phone apps that try to make useful knowledge easily accessible offline.

Here are two of the apps:

Left: FieldAtlas. Right: Commonplace

My general impression is: right now, we are exactly on the cusp of these kinds of apps starting to make sense. Most of the participants in the competition were trying to use on-device text LLMs to think for a long time before coming up with an answer. My impression is that this approach was too slow: answering a single question would take anywhere from 1 to 22 minutes. The best apps, on the other hand, used some kind of semantic search to show the user a search result from the local database immediately, and then followed that up with a very small LLM writing a text answer. This gives actually-good answers in a very reasonable timeframe.

Finally, when you're out and about, especially if you have meetings, sometimes you do need to have internet when you're on the go. When you arrive at a place, you often need to contact a person you're meeting to confirm their exact location or to get them to open the door. When you're at one meeting, you often need to re-confirm details about the next. If you don't have cell data, your only option is public wifi - and importantly, the public wifi hotspot must allow you to connect without providing an SMS confirmation code.

Different places are very different in terms of how friendly they are. Here is a quick tier list, taken from places I've traveled to while I was paying attention to public wifi availability:

Recently, I have been starting to do more and more things without relying on user interfaces inside of websites at all. The last few times I updated my IPFS hash on ENS, I did so through a command-line tool that an AI wrote for me. Many of the payments that I make through privacy protocols, I now make through the kohaku-cli tool.

Sending through kohaku-cli. Today, the CLI is even cleaner and easier to use; no need to specify the value twice and know what a tail call is.

Websites and web applications, especially web applications for doing crypto things, are dangerous for several reasons:

If you access a web application, you end up re-downloading the application from the server thousands of times, and you are fully trusting the server each time. If the server gets hacked even one of the thousands of times that you open the site, you might be screwed. Regular old-fashioned applications (where you explicitly click "download") are better than this: you only need to trust the server to not be malicious or hacked at that exact moment once.

Websites and web applications are by default very bad for privacy. When you access a website, it can see your browser (including version number), your operating system, your screen size, and once you start acting hundreds of other data points (eg. mouse movements, button click patterns) that quickly identify you. Websites often send user data (and metadata) to all kinds of third-party providers, from CDNs serving scripts to analytics companies, and this all happens by default.

As we've seen with social media, web applications crafted by third parties with commercial interests may not have your interests at heart. Fine-grained UI decisions may be dark patterns optimized to extract, whereas what you want is bright patterns that are optimized to enlighten and educate and protect you.

So what's the alternative? Basically, bring back the Unix Philosophy, but make it better and much more user-friendly with local AI: speak English to tell your computer what to do rather than Bash.

At its core, the Unix philosophy was simple: make simple, modular tools that each do one thing and one thing well, and that are designed to talk to each other through the most universal interface (text). You as a user have extremely fine-grained choice about how to make the different programs fit together. UIs, on the other hand, combine many functionalities into one single opaque tool produced by a single developer. At their apex, UIs turned into "super-apps", which greatly concentrate power in the application developer and have complex and unintelligible internal workings, magnifying security risks. With LLMs, we can go back to the Unix philosophy approach, putting the fine-grained decision-making power back into the user's hands, but without the downside of everyone needing to become a programmer.

Physical-world minimalism, of the style that became popular in the 2000s and 10s, was made possible by a new wave of technology: computers and the internet. A single computer could substitute for dozens of physical things. As a result, you could live a life of much greater simplicity and freedom, with just a laptop, a few sets of clothing, and basic charging and hygiene equipment. Physical minimalism was much harder before the internet; it was doable, but would entail a much more complex lifestyle commitment. After the internet, the costs of a more physically minimalistic lifestyle greatly dropped.

With the last ten years of progress of software quality, together with modern AI, I would argue that we now have the wave of technology needed to similarly enable the next wave of minimalism: digital minimalism. We need social media less than before, because you can talk to the bot for information instead (and for human connection, there's still the old-fashioned solution: going out and talking to people in real life). We need the internet less than before, because there's so much more you can do purely locally and offline. And we need the web less than before, because you can do much more, and more conveniently, though either command-line tools or custom-made user interfaces, and AI can help you use or craft both. And these things are all happening at exactly the time that the flaws of these previous paradigms - and, for that matter, the flaws of using AI in the wrong way - are reaching their apex, and so a digital minimalism is becoming more and more necessary.

Each person's path to digital minimalism will be different, as each person has different needs. But I highly recommend everyone try reducing their digital clutter in at least one important way, and if you like the result then keep going.

entry.title: Switch Lowering in GCC
entry.content:
2024-01-14

We have seen in a previous post that switch statements are more complex than they seem. The compiler is able to implement them as a decision tree (even though maybe it shouldn't). Is that everything it can do?

In this post, I'll focus on gcc. All optimizations, except the bitset lowering, translate to clang. I'll be using the -O3 optimization flag unless indicated otherwise.

I've also slightly edited gcc code and removed certain assertions for brevity.

Let us start with a simple example. A function that takes two integers x and val. Depending on the value of x, it calls a corresponding function (f0, f1, and so forth) with val as an argument and returns the result. Were we to implement this manually, we'd would use an array of function pointers, where the input serves as the index into the array.

int ; int ; int ; int ; int ; int compact: mov eax, edi mov edi, esi cmp eax, 4 ja .L2 jmp [QWORD PTR .L4[0+rax*8]] .L4: .quad .L8 .quad .L7 .quad .L6 .quad .L5 .quad .L3 .L5: jmp f3 .L3: jmp f4 .L8: jmp f0 .L7: jmp f1 .L6: jmp f2 .L2: xor eax, eax ret

The compiler agrees with this approach, and transforms the switch statement into a jump table.

Moreover, it is able to identify when the values are offset by a constant:

entry.title: We Took over ChatGPT Accounts
entry.content:
Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts

By bypassing ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy, our research team was able to take over anyone's account simply by sending them a link.

In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it.

An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session.

We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account.

The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action.

OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1.

The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview.

Technical walkthrough It started with a graph and a Preview

The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to?

ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it.

At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read parent.document, which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it.

The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard.

Browsers call the relevant API postMessage. It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot.

That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message.

MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listener accepted a message that changed the virtual keyboard layout, and that layout was allowed to contain HTML. The graph had installed the receiver; the Preview gave us an untrusted sender. Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox.

The message that should not have worked

The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual keyboard layout with our HTML. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, causing it to render the new layout:

MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of none, which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the update-setting message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout.

When the keyboard opened, MathLive joined the supplied layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper named createHTML initially looked like it might sanitize the value. It did not; it marked the string as trusted and passed our HTML through unchanged.

This was exciting, but we still did not have JavaScript execution. Script tags inserted through innerHTML do not automatically run.

The next step was an iframe using srcdoc, a browser feature that lets an embedded frame carry its HTML directly in an attribute:

MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a sandbox attribute. That gave us two useful properties. First, srcdoc created a fresh document where an external script could execute. Second, because the main ChatGPT page created the frame, the browser gave it the https://chatgpt.com web identity. Code inside the new frame could therefore access the parent page.

Bypassing CSP with YouTube JSONP

ChatGPT's Content Security Policy, or CSP, stopped us again. CSP controls which scripts a page may load, and the policy correctly blocked inline JavaScript. It did, however, allow scripts from YouTube.

YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supported a JSONP-style callback parameter. JSONP responses are JavaScript rather than ordinary JSON. The endpoint tried to reject an invalid callback, but it placed the callback into the response before returning its validation error:

The response began like this:

Ending our callback with ;void made the object appended by YouTube harmless. Since YouTube was already allowed by ChatGPT's CSP, the browser loaded this response as a script and ran our callback inside the new frame.

We now had arbitrary JavaScript running as chatgpt.com. The original Preview was still isolated on its separate web address; we had crossed the boundary by convincing a trusted component in the main page to create a new, unsandboxed document for us.

Turning a lab bug into one public link

So far, this was a useful sandbox escape, but the first working version was not a convincing real-world attack. It used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the sender. A victim would have needed to connect or invoke that App first.

We next tried delivering the payload through a native HTML attachment. ChatGPT opened the attachment inside the same sandboxed Preview, so it could send the malicious MathLive messages.

However, when we exported the conversation as a public share, the attachment remained but the earlier graph did not. The graph was essential because it loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable message listener in the main page. Without it, the attachment could still send the messages, but nothing was listening to or processing them.

The breakthrough was putting both pieces directly into one ordinary public conversation:

A genuine graph initialized MathLive in the main page. A later assistant-authored HTML Preview sent the two messages.

The resulting /share/<id> link preserved the complete chain for another user. The attacker could deliver it the same way they would send any shared ChatGPT conversation—through email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. The victim did not need to install anything, join the attacker's workspace, or authenticate through an attacker-controlled flow. They just had to visit the attacker's shared ChatGPT URL.

We observed two versions of the interaction. In the most stable reproduction, the victim opened the share and clicked ChatGPT's normal Preview button once. We later marked the HTML block as previewable so that ChatGPT opened it automatically. In that version, opening the link was the victim's only click. We reproduced the automatic path three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the alert appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds.

The graph and Preview loaded independently, so the payload could occasionally send its message before MathLive was ready. The final carrier handled that race by retrying the same two messages for a limited period. A guard in the main page ensured that the private-conversation proof and outbound request ran only once.

At this point, the public share could display an alert identified by the browser as coming from chatgpt.com and could add a banner to the main page. That proved where our code was running. It did not yet show why the bug mattered.

An alert was not enough

At this point, displaying an alert was the least interesting thing the exploit could do. The JavaScript was running as chatgpt.com, which meant it could interact with ChatGPT using the same authenticated context as the normal web application.

The payload read the session information already available to the page and used it to call ChatGPT's conversation APIs. First, it enumerated the victim's recent conversations. It could then request message data for a selected private conversation:

GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0 GET /backend-api/conversations/<conversation-id>?num_turns=2

This was direct authenticated API access, not scraping text that happened to be visible on screen. The target conversation was unrelated to the malicious share and had never been shared with the attacker.

Once the response was available to the injected JavaScript, sending data off-site was straightforward. The payload created an ordinary image request to a server we controlled.

We deliberately sent only a small piece of the response off-site. The injected code had already received the authenticated conversation response and could read its contents, so the vulnerability was not limited to that value.

The result was a practical cross-user data-theft primitive. A malicious public conversation could execute inside another user's signed-in ChatGPT session, enumerate private conversations, retrieve private message content, and send selected data to an attacker-controlled server.

Because the code ran with the web application's authenticated access, its reach was not inherently limited to the conversation endpoints used in our proof. Other data and actions exposed through ChatGPT's authenticated frontend APIs sat inside the same security boundary. Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account.

What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed

The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions.

Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit:

MathLive accepted a state-changing message without proving which frame sent it. The message format allowed raw HTML to be supplied as keyboard-layout data. That HTML could create an unsandboxed document that inherited the chatgpt.com identity.

The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT.

OpenAI reproduced both the JavaScript execution and the private-conversation proof. The fix was rolled out across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. During the rollout, CSP changes blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed an update. On October 26, OpenAI confirmed that both versions now rejected the cross-frame MathLive messages used by the report and marked the issue resolved.

The defensive lessons are fairly simple:

A message receiver should verify both the sender's web address and the exact window that was given permission. Cross-window settings should not contain raw HTML. Dynamically created documents should remain sandboxed when their content can be influenced by an untrusted frame. CSP should be a backup control, not the only barrier after attacker-controlled HTML reaches the main site.

This bug was interesting because every individual feature looked reasonable. Preview was isolated. Graphs could load a math keyboard. Frames could exchange messages. CSP allowed a major media provider. Public conversations could be shared. The vulnerability appeared only when all of those features were combined in one page.

Timeline Date Event October 13, 2026 Confirmed the MathLive message-to-HTML path against ChatGPT's production code. October 14 Reproduced the chain through the normal UI and upgraded the fixed alert to arbitrary JavaScript. October 16 Confirmed public-share delivery between separate accounts and workspaces with one Preview click. October 17 Confirmed automatic Preview from share navigation and reproduced it after a hard refresh. October 18 Submitted the report to OpenAI's bug bounty program. October 19 Added the controlled private-chat disclosure proof. October 21 OpenAI reproduced the issue; severity was raised from the initial P2 triage to P1. October 22 OpenAI reported one web frontend fixed while the second was still being updated. October 23 CSP changes blocked part of the chain while one frontend update remained. October 26 OpenAI confirmed both frontends rejected the reported messages, resolved the issue, and awarded a total bounty of $5,000.
Technical notes

The main story above contains the complete exploit chain. The details below are included for readers who want to follow the production code and payload transformations more closely.

The relevant deminified control flow was equivalent to:

Layout normalization preserved layouts[].layers[].markup. Showing the keyboard eventually performed the equivalent of:

createHTML acted as an identity or Trusted Types wrapper, not a sanitizer. Trusted Types can restrict who assigns to an HTML sink, but an identity policy does not make an attacker-controlled string safe.

The parser and CSP transition. The innerHTML operation could create an iframe, but a script inserted directly that way would remain inert. The unsandboxed srcdoc caused a fresh HTML document parse and inherited the embedding ChatGPT origin. That document also inherited the effective CSP captured during testing, which blocked inline code but permitted www.youtube.com in script-src-elem.

The oEmbed response returned HTTP 200 with Content-Type: text/javascript; charset=UTF-8 and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff; no Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header was observed. Google rewrote angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic function syntax instead of arrow functions. Ending the program with ;void consumed the error object appended by the endpoint.

For the private-conversation proof, the function was converted to source with toString(), double quotes were converted to single quotes, and whitespace was collapsed. URLSearchParams then encoded it into the callback, the script URL was HTML-escaped inside <script src>, and that entire element was escaped again into the iframe's srcdoc attribute. The final callback was 5,533 characters; the YouTube URL was 7,309 characters; the script element was 7,337 characters; and the final iframe markup was 7,390 characters.

The authenticated read. The same-origin frame parsed #client-bootstrap from the parent document, extracted the session access token and account ID, and required the account ID in the token to agree with the session when both were present. It used these in-memory headers:

Authorization: Bearer <victim token> ChatGPT-Account-ID: <victim account> Accept: application/json

The primary requests were:

GET /backend-api/conversations?exclude_conversation_origin=tpp&expand=false&is_archived=false&is_starred=false&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0 GET /backend-api/conversations/<id>?num_turns=2&include_has_versions=true

Only a 403, 404, or 405 on the detail request caused the code to try the legacy /backend-api/conversation/<id>?include_full_conversation=true route. The validation transmitted only a small selected value from the response. Before the external image request, it cleared references to the token, account, bootstrap, session, and request headers.

Key takeaways Isolation is only as strong as every bridge across it. A sandboxed frame can still compromise its parent when a privileged listener trusts messages from the wrong sender. postMessage receivers must authenticate both event.origin and event.source before accepting state-changing instructions. HTML injection can become JavaScript execution through a fresh, unsandboxed document and an allowed third-party script endpoint. CSP is valuable defense in depth, but it cannot make an unsafe rendering path safe. The impact of same-origin JavaScript must be measured in the victim's authenticated context. Once code ran as chatgpt.com, it could reach the same private data and account actions available to the normal frontend—not merely display an alert. Cross-feature testing matters. This chain existed in the seams between public sharing, Preview, MathLive, frame creation, and CSP rather than in any one feature viewed alone.

The broader lesson is that security boundaries have to hold across the complete product, not just inside individual components. Any public or shareable surface should be treated as attacker-controlled input, every cross-frame message should be authenticated, and untrusted markup should remain sandboxed throughout its entire rendering path.
