4 Discussion

ParticleDB 1.1.4 claimed to be a Postgres-compatible database which offered Snapshot Isolation with its occ-v3 and zero-copy-occ transaction modes, Serializability with serializable-ssi, and Strong Serializability with table-2pl.

Instead, we found a library of confusion.10 In versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-19, basic functionality like transactions (#3), prepared statements (#2), and Postgres auth (#1) were unusably broken. The server spontaneously deadlocked (#27, #71) or crashed (#81) every few minutes. Integers stood in for booleans (#30, #50), comparisons to NULL threw errors (#13), and you could assign multiple values to the same column (#5). Large floating-point numbers quietly became infinite (#56); Infinity, NaN, and NULL arithmetic were broken (#36, #92, #15, #21); and out-of-range values were improperly stored or clipped to fit (#32, #11). In ParticleDB, 0.0 was not equal to 0 (#63), but 0.90... wasnât not equal to 5 (#80). Strings allowed too many (#52, #64) and too few (#55) characters. A WHERE clause with floating-point operations would silently fail to match any rows (#47), WHERE 4 = 5 returned rows with primary key 5 (#18), WHERE a = 1 matched the row {a: 2}, and WHERE TRUE matched nothing (#35). Null (#8) and unique (#9) constraints did nothing, and primary keys could be duplicated (#29), null (#57), or both. Primary keys failed to conflict with rows that did exist (#90), and conflicted with rows that didnât (#82). Joins returned incorrect column names (#54), coerced values to strings (#76), failed to return rows (#59), and confused similarly-named columns (#77). It was impossible to delete rows within a transaction (#26, #45), rows with integers set to floats (#23), or with floats set to integers (#84), or those containing NaNs (#78), or fixed-width strings (#74).11 Rows from dropped tables could re-emerge in mangled forms (#46). Columns could be set to values of the wrong type, silently altering or corrupting data (#7). Inserts ignored provided columns, creating rows best described as âdeeply cursedâ (#16).12 Updates could create new, shambolic rows where none existed (#24, #25). Strings sometimes turned into eight-bit integers (#37), and primary keys occasionally became NULL (#72). Aborted transactions could commit, or fail with their effects still visible (#43). Queries sometimes missed (#48), duplicated (#89), or returned the wrong (#67) rows. Tables with a text primary key were mostly invisible (#41). Special values were sometimes inalterable (#91). Entire columns occasionally vanished for no obvious reason (#65). Uncontended statements on freshly created tables observed nonsensical results or conflicted (apparently) with themselves (#31). Each transaction and WAL mode exhibited essentially every transactional anomaly our tests could detect: write loss, internal consistency violations, G0, G1a, G1b, G1c, G-Single, G-nonadjacent, P4, A5A, G2, and real-time variants thereof (#38, #66, #68, #69, #73, #70, #96, #109, #110, etc.).

These behaviors occurred in single-node instances of ParticleDB, without fault injection, often with just a single client. When we killed ParticleDB, it allowed internal anomalies, P4 (Lost Update), and G-single (#107), even with the new serializable transaction mode. Corruption or truncation of WAL files caused partial data loss (#108). Simulating misdirected reads or writes could cause total data loss (#112).

As we concluded our engagement, version 1.1.18.11.rc-22 had just become available. It abandoned the table-2pl and serializable-ssi transaction modes in favor of fast, occ, and serializable, which were intended to offer no consistency, Snapshot Isolation, and Strong Serializability, respectively. While 1.1.18.11.rc-22 was significantly safer than 1.1.4, we were still finding new issues. The default occ mode regularly lost data in normal operation (#110). The new serializable mode appeared significantly safer, but still allowed stale read (#109) in normal operation, and with process kills, sometimes failed to read extant rows. This led to internal anomalies, Lost Update, and more (#107).

After we finished testing, Orkes updated ParticleDBâs documentation to claim that every transaction mode discussed here was âexperimentalâ. This claim is difficult to support. To the best of Jepsenâs knowledge, none of the ParticleDB documentation described these modes as experimental or unsupported during our engagement. Orkesâ unpublished operator guide did describe one mode, serializable-occ, as an âinternal A/B variantâ¦ do not use for correctness runsâ. We considered that mode experimental and omitted it from this report. However, the others had no such caveats.

Orkes appears to have reworked ParticleDBâs approach to consistency. It now supports the standard SQL isolation level statements for READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ (meaning Snapshot Isolation), and SERIALIZABLE. The --txn-mode option is gone, and a new --concurrency-control setting has none, optimistic, and strict-optimistic options. The documentation claims that every mode discussed in this report has been removed from version 1.1.19-rc.13. However, it goes on to say that occ-v3 and strict-serializable were âearlier namesâ of the âoptimistic engineâ and âstrict serializable modeâ, respectively. It is not clear whether these modes were removed or simply renamed.

Jepsen has not evaluated versions of ParticleDB after 1.1.18.11.rc-22, and cannot speak to these isolation levels or concurrency control modes. However, Orkes claims that all issues from this report have been addressed as of version 1.1.19-rc.13.

As always, Jepsen takes an experimental approach to safety verification: we can prove the presence of bugs, but not their absence. While we make extensive efforts to find problems, we cannot prove correctness.

4.1 Impact

Orkes believes that the issues we found in 1.1.4 were likely due to an extensive refactor of ParticleDB in spring 2026, and that Orkes and their customers, who continued to run an earlier version, were likely unaffected. Near the end of our collaboration we briefly evaluated an internal build of version 1.0.0. While it exhibited some string and arithmetic issues, that version did not seem susceptible to most of the serious safety errors we found in 1.1.4, and passed cursory rw and append tests. We tested only a single node at a time, so we cannot speak to the safety of the replication system.

From May through July 2026, the ParticleDB download page offered users (at least) versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-18.13 All exhibited serious safety errors during normal operation. It seems likely that users who ran these versions of ParticleDB would have lost or corrupted data. In version 1.1.18.11.rc-22, using WAL mode sync and transaction mode serializable significantly reduced the frequency and severity of these issues, but did not prevent internal anomalies or Lost Update.

Given the severity and extent of the safety errors we found, and the process which produced them, Jepsen recommends users halt further deployment of ParticleDB and migrate to other databases as soon as possible. Consider checking and/or rebuilding database state from more reliable sources, if available.

4.2 The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Generative Testing

The compare workload generated random schemas and SQL statements over them, then ran both against ParticleDB and Postgres to see if they produced equivalent results. This should not have worked. There are many ways in which two âPostgres-compatibleâ databases can legitimately differ, such as floating-point details, which error message takes precedence, or the order of unsorted results. The space of SQL queries is large and difficult to cover. Many queries trivially return equivalent results (e.g.Â SELECT ... WHERE FALSE) and therefore tell us little information. We can test only sequential behavior, which is easy for a databaseâs standard test suite to check.

Nevertheless, roughly two thousand lines of generative tests found a wealth of bugs in ParticleDB, and unlike Jepsenâs typical workloads, the examples generated were usually easy to reproduce. ParticleDB offered a good deal of âlow-hanging fruitâ that should have been caught by example-based testsâbut the compare workload also found more subtle errors. For example, the fact that 0.90... was apparently equal to 5 hinged on a high-precision floating-point literal. Inspired by this success, we extracted part of the ParticleDB SQL generator into a shared library so it could be used in other tests, like the new internal-sim workload.

Jepsen has traditionally focused on thorough analysis of a small set of carefully chosen transactions. This is partly because checking (e.g.) Serializability in general is NP-complete, and also because we assume that if transactions of (e.g.) reads and appends work correctly on strings, so will other operations on other datatypes. Our intuition is that the âhard partâ is in the concurrency control mechanism, and sequential datatype behavior is generally covered by existing tests. This was not the case in ParticleDB. Weâve expanded Jepsenâs list-append and rw tests to use alternate encodings and transaction structures, in an attempt to cover more codepaths. This revealed new bugs in ParticleDB, and we hope it will in other databases too.

Unfortunately, compare became less useful as Orkes fixed major bugs and left smaller incompatibilities in place. For example, Postgres checks unique constraints when updating each row of a table, but ParticleDB only checks after all have been updated. This means that a statement like UPDATE bools SET x = NOT x can swap the values of TRUE and FALSE in ParticleDB without violating a unique constraint. Toward the end of our engagement, the compare test generally hit these minor inconsistencies early, then spent most of its time searching for minimal cases of themâpotentially missing more serious bugs.

4.3 Quality Assurance

Orkes said they ran Jepsenâs existing Postgres test harness to find and resolve issues in ParticleDB prior to this work. However, that same test harness failed immediately when run against ParticleDB 1.1.4. Orkes also stated they tested ParticleDB with SQLancer, which generates far more complex queries than the ones we tested. It is therefore perplexing that nearly every feature we tested exhibited glaring errors, and that our findings seemed to come as a surprise.

Most databases have a test suite which exercises at least basic examples of each feature, and it is customary to run those tests before release, if not continuously. Where were those tests for ParticleDB? How does one add support for NOT NULL constraints without a test which tries to insert at least one NULL value? What development process adds a CHARACTER(10) type without trying to write a string of (e.g.) five characters?

Our findings suggest structural deficiencies in the ParticleDB QA process. Perhaps tests were not run prior to release. Perhaps the test suite was run, but failed to exercise basic functionality. Perhaps engineers entrusted Large Language Models with the work of testing.

Jepsen recommends that Orkes (and all database vendors!) build and exercise an automated test suite for their database. This suite should include at least simple, example-based tests covering important database features. These tests should fail when the feature is unimplemented or malformed, and pass when it is complete. Observing these failures is an important part of the development process: it validates that the test measures something. Tests should be run at least once before each release, and results disseminated to the team. Afterwards consider more sophisticated generative tests, establishing adversarial QA and implementation teams, and subtly breaking safety mechanisms to determine whether the tests are still effective.

4.4 Documentation

ParticleDBâs website gave the appearance of a mature database project. It made strong claims: a general-purpose OLTP/OLAP SQL database a thousand times faster than PostgreSQL, âformally verifiedâ by a TLA+ proof, multiple APIs, and client libraries in thirteen languages. It offered a variety of deployment options and extensive documentation on database features and operations.

On closer inspection, that documentation was riddled with omissions, inconsistencies, and confabulations. The TLA+ proof was not published, and in any event did not prevent disasterâperhaps it was incorrect, formalized the wrong properties, or did not describe the system as built. Safety-critical configuration settings like the transaction mode were described in vague terms, like âsafe under concurrencyâ. The documentation for the Java client library referred to non-existent dependency coordinates and seemed to make up class and package names which were nowhere to be found in the library itself. The quickstart and client examples made up a variety of default usernames for ParticleDB, all of which were wrong. The stored procedure documentation even fabricated an imaginary email address for the author of this report. In Orkesâ unpublished operator guide, the descriptions of transaction modes omitted basic phenomena like G0 and confused G1a (Aborted Read) with G1c (Circular Information Flow). The Snapshot Isolation modes made no mention of G-single or the other boundary phenomena proscribed by Snapshot Isolation, and non-real-time models made no mention of the real-time phenomena they allowed, like Stale Read.14

Technical writing is important work that requires skill and care. Jepsen recommends that Orkes work with a human technical writer to rewrite ParticleDBâs documentation, with an eye toward concisely and accurately communicating intended behavior and the guarantees users should expect.

Jepsen is no stranger to working with early software projects, and there is nothing intrinsically wrong with offering buggy or badly broken software. However, it would be polite for a maintainer aware of serious safety issues to display a prominent warning on the website. One might place a large red box on the download page which reads, âThis project is in early development and is not suitable for productionâ, or more bluntly, âThis software has lost data and will do so againâ. Orkes should clearly explain the general status of ParticleDB, and advise users of specific known safety issues.

Orkes has since published a release history which describes versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 as âunsupported pre-release buildsâ. It is not clear how users would have understood versions like 1.1.4 or 1.1.18.9 as âpre-releaseâ. Pre-release software generally has a version number beginning with 0, or including ârcâ, âalphaâ, etc. The documentation did not describe these versions as pre-release or experimental at the time. Indeed, the Docker install page told users how to deploy these versions âfor productionâ.

4.5 LLM Tradeoffs

Large Language Models enable small teams to produce software and documentation of staggering scope and complexity in a remarkably short time. Five years ago, writing a distributed SQL database of this scope might have taken hundreds of person-years.15 With LLM assistance, a handful of engineers at Orkes were able to produce a highly sophisticated database system.

However, our work on ParticleDB (and other databases) suggests there are serious tradeoffs to relying on LLMs. Quality suffered: ParticleDB was a fractal of correctness errors. LLM tooling repeatedly claimed that bugs had been fixed when, in fact, they had not. ParticleDB also seemed more difficult to understand than typical databases. As with most Jepsen analyses, Orkes engineers offered detailed explanations of the causes and resolutions of the bugs we found in Conductor. However, Orkes seemed unable to explain the causes or resolutions of nearly every issue we found in ParticleDB. New builds simply materialized, sans changelogs, each hopefully containing a slew of improvements. Why did ParticleDB sometimes turn strings into integers? Why did it stop in 1.1.18.11.rc-1? Perhaps no one knows. With LLMs, perhaps no one needs to.

More broadly, the use of LLMs erodes trust in documentation, in software, and in the organizations which produce them. Perhaps engineers will begin to treat any new software project with suspicionâthe signals we used to rely on as markers of a mature system are now easier to counterfeit.

Where correctness mattersâand surely it ought to matter for databases!âour industry must acknowledge and mitigate these tradeoffs.16 In the age of LLMs, what can maintainers do to ensure correct software and accurate documentation? Having done that work, how can they demonstrate its quality to users?

4.6 Future Work

As of 1.1.18.11.rc-22, our append and rw workloads were still finding anomalies in every transaction mode. We recommend further testing as development continues. The compare workload also revealed a number of minor compatibility bugs which we have not discussed here. These small differences could mask more serious errors. Bringing ParticleDB into closer alignment with Postgres could help the compare workload reveal them.

Toward the end of our collaboration we tested ParticleDBâs on-disk format, and found that corruption in WAL files could cause data loss. The variety of error messages we found suggests that there might be multiple paths to data lossâfurther tests should stress on-disk storage more thoroughly. Furthermore, in almost all our tests ParticleDB wrote only WAL files, and stored its tables entirely in memory. We recommend Orkes add a configuration option to reduce the thresholds for on-disk storage, so that future tests can exercise those codepaths.

The ParticleDB client has a number of slow network timeouts we did not know how to change. These timeouts could conceal safety errors by preventing the test from observing the database during a critical moment. We worked around this by using the Postgres client (whose timeouts are configurable), but we recommend testing the ParticleDB client with lower timeouts as well.

ParticleDB offered a massive set of features, and we only tested a small portion of them. The SQL specification and Postgresâ dialect of it are astonishingly complex languages, and we used only a small fraction of their syntax and vocabulary. We also did not evaluate ParticleDBâs Redis or HTTP APIs, temporal or geospatial queries, materialized views, vector search, or multi-tenant features. The replication system remains to be tested.

Orkes is now adding stored procedures to ParticleDB. These user-defined functions, called Particles, are written in Python or Rust and executed by the database server. Both Rust and Python have large surface areas, and executing user-provided binaries in a database environment seems like an exciting opportunity. Our previous work with stored procedures suggests this feature is worth further investigation.

ParticleDB claimed to be â1087x faster than PostgreSQLâ. In our tests ParticleDB was nowhere near this fast, and over the course of an hour we observed a linear decline in throughput and a significant increase in median latenciesâeven over small datasets. Once ParticleDB reaches a baseline level of correctness, revisiting performance benchmarks could be worthwhile.

Our thanks to the ParticleDB team at Orkes, including Jeu George and Nikhil Kala. Jepsen also wishes to thank Irene Kannyo for her editorial support. This research was funded by Orkes, Inc., and conducted in accordance with the Jepsen ethics policy.

5 Appendix A

This appendix contains additional results involving types, syntax, numbers, and strings.

5.1 Type Safety and Syntax

We found several incompatibilities or bugs involving static or dynamic type safety, or behaviors that would normally have been caught by static analysis of a query, such as referring to a nonexistent column. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults.

5.1.1 Ordering By an Unused Column (#33)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, you could order an aggregate queryâs results by a column that was not used in the aggregate expressions or GROUP BY clause. This seems like a minor issue, but it does differ from Postgres behavior:

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a boolean); root=> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE (a >= a) ORDER BY a LIMIT 0; COUNT ------- (0 rows)

Orkes resolved this issue (#33) in 1.1.18.9.

5.1.2 Comparison of Incomparable Types (#6)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, you could write predicates for UPDATE and DELETE which made equality comparisons between columns of different types.

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a text, b smallint); root=> DELETE FROM t WHERE (a = b); DELETE 0

In Postgres, this threw an error like ERROR: operator does not exist: text = smallint. You could compare strings to boolean columns, or literal values like false. ParticleDB allowed these comparisons on empty tables, but would throw an error if a record was present. In 1.1.18.6, ParticleDB threw an error for empty tables as well (#6).

5.1.3 Cannot Compare Decimals to Floats (#94)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2 forgot how to compare large decimal literals to 64-bit floating-point numbers:

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a double precision); root=> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (1.0); root=> SELECT * FROM t WHERE ((0 / 1.2002480805601245E26) >= t.a); ERROR: arrow compute: Invalid argument error: Invalid comparison operation: Decimal256(76, 44) >= Float64

This issue (#94) no longer appeared by version 1.1.18.11.rc-18.

5.1.4 Filter Predicates Reject NULL (#12)

SQL has three boolean values: TRUE, FALSE, and NULL, which represents an unknown value. In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, predicates in SELECT, UPDATE, etc. could not evaluate to NULL, even though the SQL specification states that search conditions are boolean expressions. For example:

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a boolean); root=> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (TRUE); root=> SELECT * FROM t WHERE NULL; ERROR: filter predicate must produce boolean result

In Postgres this would return an empty relation, because NULL is not TRUE. In 1.1.18.6, NULL predicates evaluated correctly (#12).

5.1.5 Cannot Compare Values to NULL (#13)

Per the ANSI SQL standard, the value of comparing anything to NULL is unknown, represented as the boolean value NULL. However, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 sometimes refused to evaluate predicates which compared (e.g.) integers to NULL.

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a int); root=> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (2), (NULL); root=> UPDATE t SET a = 5 WHERE a = NULL; ERROR: arrow compute: Invalid argument error: Invalid comparison operation: Int64 == Null

Oddly enough, ParticleDB correctly evaluated statements like SELECT 1 = NULL. Version 1.1.18.6 correctly compared integers to NULL (#13).

5.1.6 Boolean Logic on Integers (#30)

The SQL standard is clear that boolean logical expressions like A AND B evaluate to booleans. In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, they could sometimes be other things:

root=> SELECT TRUE AND 5; # => 5 root=> SELECT 5 AND TRUE; # => 5 root=> SELECT 5 AND FALSE; # => FALSE root=> SELECT 5 OR TRUE; # => TRUE root=> SELECT 'cat' OR FALSE; # => 'cat' root=> SELECT 'cat' OR 'dog'; ERROR: OR requires boolean operands root=> SELECT 1 AND 2; ERROR: AND conjunct must produce boolean

By version 1.1.18.9, ParticleDB rejected boolean expressions over non-boolean literals (#30).

5.1.7 More Boolean/Integer Confusion (#50)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 disallowed boolean logic on integer literals, but allowed it on columns.

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a int); root=> UPDATE t SET a = NOT a; UPDATE 0

Likewise, you could do integer operations on booleans:

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a boolean); root=> UPDATE t SET a = ((a + a) IS NULL) WHERE a; UPDATE 0

Orkes seems to have resolved this issue (#50) by version 1.1.18.11.rc-8.

5.1.8 Multiple Assignment to a Single Column (#5)

The SQL standard specifies that an UPDATE statement shall not contain a column name more than once. However, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 allowed an UPDATE to assign multiple values to the same column. It seemed to pick the last value, lexically.

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a boolean, b boolean); root=> INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (FALSE, FALSE); root=> UPDATE t SET a = FALSE, a = TRUE; UPDATE 1

In Postgres this returned an error: multiple assignments to same column "a". However, ParticleDB applied the update, producing:

root=> select * from t; a | b ---+--- t | f (1 row)

By version 1.1.18.6, multiple updates to the same column threw an error (#5).

5.1.9 Predicates Referring to Non-Existent Columns (#10)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17, predicates in SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements could refer to columns which did not exist. For example:

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a INT); root=> SELECT * FROM t WHERE b = 1; a --- (0 rows)

In Postgres, expressions like this would throw ERROR: column "b" does not exist. By version 1.1.18.6, ParticleDB did as well (#10).

5.2 Arithmetic

ParticleDB often performed arithmetic in unexpected ways. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults.

5.2.1 No Large Integer Literals (#14)

Postgres allows large integer literals like 9223372036854775808 (263). However, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 refused these literals, throwing an invalid integer error:

root=> SELECT 9223372036854775808; ERROR: invalid integer: 9223372036854775808

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.6, one could write large integer literals (#14).

5.2.2 To Infinity, and Beyond (#85)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 gained an exponentiation operator ^, but could not apply it to Infinity.

SELECT 'Infinity' ^ 2;

This returned 'Infinity' in Postgres, but threw operator does not exist: ^ requires numeric operands in ParticleDB. By 1.1.18.11.rc-9, Orkes seems to have resolved this issue (#85).

5.2.3 -1 ^ 0 = -1 (#49)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 considered -1 ^ 0 to be equal to -1, rather than 1.

root=> select -1 ^ 0; -1 ---- -1 (1 row)

By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, it correctly returned 1 (#49).

5.2.4 1.0 + 1E-39 = 1.0 (#88)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.6 gained support for literals using scientific notationâfor example, using 3E12 to denote 3âÃâ1012. However, the parser turned this notation into floating-point values, rather than precise decimals, as in Postgres. This resulted in floating-point errors:

root=> SELECT 1.0 + 1E-39 = 1.0; ?column? ---------- t (1 row)

This issue (#88) was fixed by 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2.

5.2.5 Whatâs the Largest Number You Can Think Of? (#56)

ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-1 silently converted large floating-point literals to infinities:

root=> SELECT -4.56E500; ?column? ----------- -Infinity (1 row)

By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, ParticleDB threw an error like "4.56E500" is out of range for type double precision (#56).

5.2.6 Exponent Underflow (#61)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.9, the exponent operator checked to see if its arguments would cause an overflow, but did not check for underflow:

root=> SELECT 200 ^ 200; ERROR: value out of range: overflow root=> SELECT -200 ^ -200; -0 ---- 0 (1 row)

By version 1.1.18.11.rc-3, ParticleDB threw an underflow error (#61).

5.2.7 Division by Integer Zero (#34)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, you could divide floating-point values by integer 0 and receive Infinity, rather than a division by zero error, as in Postgres.

root=> SELECT 1.0 / 0; 1 / 0 ------- inf (1 row)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 returned an error instead (#34).

5.2.8 Modulo Operator Cannot Handle Floats (#51)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.9, the modulo operator % threw an internal error when either argument was a floating-point number.

root=> SELECT 3.0 % 2; ERROR: internal error

The MOD function was unaffected, and this issue (#51) was fixed by 1.1.18.11.rc-1.

5.2.9 Broken NaN Arithmetic (#36)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8, arithmetic operations on NaN would throw an error:

root=> SELECT 'NaN' - 1.0; ERROR: arrow compute: Invalid argument error: Invalid arithmetic operation: Utf8 - Float64

By 1.1.18.9, arithmetic on NaN correctly returned NaN (#36).

5.2.10 Broken NULL Arithmetic (#92)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-9.2, arithmetic operations involving sufficiently detailed scientific notation literals and NULL threw internal errors:

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a int); root=> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (NULL); root=> SELECT * FROM t WHERE (t.a + 2.0000000000000000E-23) IS NULL; ERROR: internal error: called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value (at crates/exec/...)

This error (#92) no longer appeared in version 1.1.18.11.rc-18.

5.2.11 UPDATE Canât Do Math (#60)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 introduced a new bug which rendered it unable to do arithmetic operations on floating-point columns in an UPDATE statement.17 For example:

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a real); CREATE TABLE root=> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (1.2); INSERT 0 1 root=> UPDATE t SET a = a + 1; ERROR: internal error

In 1.1.18.11.rc-1, ParticleDB was (mostly) able to add numbers (#60).

5.2.12 Same Precision For real and double precision (#32)

Per the SQL standard, the double precision data type should have a greater precision than real. In Postgres, real and double precision are (usually) a 32-bit and 64-bit floating-point value, respectively. In ParticleDB, both appear to be implemented as 64-bit floats.

CREATE TABLE t (a real NOT NULL); INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (4.134917993754883E8); SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY a; ParticleDB: [{:a 4.134917993754883E8}] Postgres: [{:a 4.134918E8}]

Version 1.1.18.9 seemed to introduce a 32-bit real type (#32).

5.2.13 Big Integers (#11)

Similarly, integer fields (e.g.Â smallint, int, â¦) in ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.17 allowed values much bigger than their typical ranges. It appeared as if ParticleDB internally represented all integer types as signed 64-bit integers. For example, here are four values too big to fit in a Postgres smallint:

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a smallint); root=> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (32768); root=> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (9223372036854775807); root=> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (9223372036854775808); root=> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (1.234E40); root=> SELECT * FROM t; a --------------------- 32768 9223372036854775807 0 9223372036854775807 (5 rows)

In Postgres smallint is a 16-bit integer; each INSERT would throw ERROR: smallint out of range. However, ParticleDB stored each of these values with varying results. It preserved 32,768 and 263âââ1 (the largest twoâs-complement signed 64-bit integer). 263 and larger integers were silently converted to 0. On the other hand, the large floating-point number was clipped to 263âââ1.

Similar behavior occurred with int and bigint. ParticleDB 1.1.18.6 rejected oversized integers (#11).

5.2.14 Dividing Nearby Numbers (#86)

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 through 1.1.18.11.rc-8 struggled to divide floating-point numbers, often throwing Numeric out of range when asked to divide values which were well within the range of a 32-bit float. For example:

root=> SELECT 81938.0 / 81937.82012987136848; ERROR: numeric out of range

This value should be approximately 1.00000219. Orkes seems to have resolved this issue (#86) in version 1.1.18.11.rc-9.

5.2.15 Floating-Point Errors in Integer Values (#87)

In ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 through 1.1.18.11.rc-8, adding small numbers (e.g. 0.1) to large integer columns could cause their values to change by surprising amounts. For example:

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a bigint); root=> INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (58950791971326900); root=> UPDATE t SET a = (a + 1E-1); root=> SELECT a FROM t; a ------------------- 58950791971326896

Adding 0.1 to this column actually subtracted 4. Jepsen suspects this bug (#87) was caused by performing these operations on floating-point values (which cannot represent all integers) then coercing the result back to the nearest integer value. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-9 seems to have fixed this.

5.2.16 Floats Are Not Equal to Quoted Forms (#19)

Postgres considers floating-point numbers like 0.0 to be equal to their quoted representationsâthis is useful because some floating-point values, like 'Infinity', are written with quotes. ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 thought otherwise:

root=> SELECT 0.0 = '0.0'; false ------- f (1 row)

This issue (#19) appeared resolved as of version 1.1.18.6.

5.2.17 Floats Are Not Equal to Integers (#63)

In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.6, floats were not equal to integers.

root=> SELECT 0.0 = 0; false ------- f (1 row)

By version 1.1.18.8, reasonably-sized integers were equal to their floating-point counterparts (#63).

5.2.18 Double Precision Floats Appear Equal to Almost All Integers (#80)

Version 1.1.18.9 introduced a new bug which made predicates like WHERE x != y fail to match for most double precision floats in (-1.0, 1.0). It was as if all small floats were equal to all nonzero integers. If we took a table containing a few integers, and performed some simple queries that should return every rowâ¦

CREATE TABLE t (a int); INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (-1), (0), (5); SELECT * FROM t WHERE a != (0.1 ^ 25); SELECT * FROM t WHERE a != 0.90000000000000000000000000000000000000; SELECT * FROM t WHERE a != -0.34656654456890453890613489540952456545;

All three of these queries returned only a single row, 0âimplying that 0.90... was equal to -1 and 5. The only exception seemed to be WHERE a != 0.0..., which returned no rows at all. This was also wrong, but somewhat less so. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-9 seems to have resolved the matter (#80).

5.3 Strings

We found several problems with strings in ParticleDB, including datatypes that could hold more or fewer characters than they ought, and improper sort orders. These issues occurred with a single server, single client, and no faults.

5.3.1 CHARACTER(n) Allows More Than n Characters (#64, #52)

The SQL standard defines a variety of fixed-width string datatypes like character(3), which holds a string of exactly three characters. Unfortunately, ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4 were happy to store much larger strings in those columns.18

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a character(3)); root=> INSERT INTO t VALUES ('large language model'); root=> SELECT * FROM t; a ---------------------- large language model (1 row)

Version 1.1.18.6 rejected inserts and updates of too-long string literals (#64), but appeared to perform these checks only at runtime; one could still say UPDATE t SET a = 'far too long' so long as it matched no rows (#52). That issue was resolved in version 1.1.18.11.rc-3.

5.3.2 CHARACTER(n) Allows Fewer Than n Characters (#55)

While 1.1.18.6 rejected strings that were too large for a fixed-width string column, 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9 also allowed strings that were too short. Normally, shorter strings are padded with spaces to the specified length, but in ParticleDB, short strings were returned unchanged.

CREATE TABLE t (a character(16)); INSERT INTO t VALUES ('smol'); SELECT * FROM t; -> {:a "smol"}

This should have returned "smol ", with padding spaces. ParticleDB 1.1.18.11.rc-1 seems to have resolved the issue (#55).

5.3.3 Default Text Collation (#22)

On a platform with LC_COLLATE = en_US.UTF-8, Postgres uses that collation by default. ParticleDB appeared to collate strings differently. Sorting via queries like SELECT ... ORDER BY name, or comparisons like 'a' < 'B', returned different results between the two databases. Where Postgres considered 'a' < 'B', ParticleDB believed the opposite.

Experiments suggest ParticleDB sorted by Unicode code point order, rather than the Unicode Collation Algorithm (UCA) with the localeâs collation rules. It may have been compatible with ucs_basic, C, or pg_c_utf8. ParticleDB version 1.1.18.9 seemed to choose a default collation more like UCA (#22).

5.3.4 Mis-Sorted Text (#42, #93)

Throughout our collaboration ParticleDB struggled to sort things. Versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 accepted an explicit unicode text collation, then ignored it:

root=> CREATE TABLE t (b text COLLATE unicode); root=> INSERT INTO t (b) VALUES ('a'), ('b'), ('B'); root=> SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY b; b --- B a b (3 rows)

In Postgresâ unicode collation, letters like a and A sort similarly, despite being of different cases. This query would have returned 'a', 'b', 'B'.

ParticleDB 1.1.18.9 sorted English uppercase and lowercase letters correctly, but only for some queriesâadding a LIMIT clause to a SELECT statement would cause it to revert to the old sort order. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 resolved that, but sorted other characters, like punctuation, oddly:

root=> CREATE TABLE t (a text COLLATE unicode); root=> INSERT INTO t VALUES ('_aa'), ('a'), ('aa'), ('aaa'); root=> SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY a ASC; a ----- a _aa aa aaa (4 rows)

Different sorting of whitespace and punctuation (#42) seemed better in version 1.1.18.11.rc-7, but reappeared in 1.1.18.11.rc-9 through 1.1.18.11.rc-19 (#93). Text sorting seemed improved in 1.1.18.11.rc-21.

There are also a handful of unrelated databases called ParticleDB, mainly used in particle physicsâfor example, the database of particles used in the Belle II physics experiment, or this one at the Large Hadron Collider.â©ï¸

The Particles feature was not available during our work; we focus on ParticleDBâs SQL interfaces.â©ï¸

One envisions a world of meta-recursive database documentation in the style of Raymond Smullyan. âOne page of the documentation always tells the truth. Another tells only liesâ¦ââ©ï¸

Presumably Two-Phase Locking.â©ï¸

With apologies to Deleuze & GuattariâThus, the tuple without fields is opposed less to fields as such than to the organization of the fields insofar as it composes a row. Le n-uplet sans composants is not a deleted tuple but a living tuple all the more alive and teeming once it has blown apart the client and its memory model. Structs commingling on the heap. Self-modifying Perl. The full tuple without fields is a tuple populated by multiplicities.â©ï¸

Madred, 2369.â©ï¸

Cameron, 1986.â©ï¸

He explained that the Databaseâthe Denormalized, the Data Lakehouse, the giant Monadâis a table without tuples. Le tableau sans n-uplets is permeated by unformed, unstable values, by dataflows in all directions, by free JSON or nomadic singletons, by mad or transitory transactions. That, however, was not the question at hand. For there simultaneously occurs upon the database a very important, inevitable phenomenon that is beneficial in many respects and unfortunate in many others: schematization. Schemata are Layers, Belts. They consist of giving form to values, of imprisoning arrays or locking singletons into systems of record and replication, of producing upon the body of the database records large and small and organizing them into normal aggregates. Schemata are acts of capture, they are like âblack holesâ or occlusions striving to seize whatever comes within their reach. They operate by coding and normalization upon the database; they proceed simultaneously by code and normality. The Schemata are judgements of God; schematization in general is the entire system of the judgement of God (but the database, or the table without tuples, constantly eludes that judgement, flees and becomes deschematized, destructured, denormalized).â©ï¸

To make matters more confusing, serializable in versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-11.2 was (depending on which version of the binary you asked) either an alias for table-2pl or possibly occ-v3. In 1.1.18.11.rc-22, serializable reappeared as a new Strong Serializable transaction mode, also based on Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), but perhaps not the serializable-ssi level present in earlier builds, which was distinct from strict-serializable.â©ï¸

De Lioncourt, 1793, presaging Borges, 1941.â©ï¸

See ANSI/NISO Z39.19-2005 (R2010) âCelestial Emporium of Benevolent Knowledgeâ for the full taxonomy of database records: rows belonging to the DBA, tombstones, those which from afar look like JSON, et cetera, etc.â©ï¸

Jepsen encourages the consistency model research community to come up with more official terms for this.â©ï¸

Running particledb --version might not return the actual version. For instance, 1.1.16 through 1.1.18.11.rc-18 all identified themselves as âspanner 1.1.16â.â©ï¸

Barthes can rejoice: not only is the author dead, but they were never alive to begin with. Nothing is true, everything is permitted.â©ï¸

MongoDB had 962 employees in 2018, and Cockroach Labs had 400 in 2022. Databases are hard!â©ï¸

Or perhaps not. Not every application requires perfect correctness. Vibrational Database Management Systems might be fine, at least some of the time.â©ï¸

Mattel, 1992.â©ï¸

Danielewski, 2000.â©ï¸

entry.title: Malware uses LLMs to rank victims by how much they're worth
entry.content:
VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value. If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails. This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator.

There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.

After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.

The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.

The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.”

VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.

Endpoint

https[:]//openrouter[.]ai/api/v1/chat/completions

Default model

anthropic/claude-opus-4.6

Fallback chain

moonshotai/kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash

Temperature

0.2 — deterministic, consistent output

Request format

Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0

Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.

The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.

The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.

Stealer capabilities

VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.

Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext.

What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.

After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.

The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated.

Deployment model

Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.

This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.

If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.

All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.

Countermeasures

Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply. 

In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device.

Conclusions

VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM, though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.

The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement.

The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.

entry.title: Ex-Meta Researcher Torrented Pirated Books, Deleted It 'Due to Litigation'
entry.content:
In a series of lawsuits in California federal court, Meta is being sued over the use of pirated books to train its Llama AI models.

The lawsuits are separate, but Judge Vince Chhabria handles them together. The plaintiffs include authors such as Sarah Silverman and Ta-Nehisi Coates, and publishers such as Entrepreneur Media and Chicken Soup for the Soul.

In August, Meta told Entrepreneur that it did not believe it had obtained the pirated Books3 dataset through BitTorrent. Books3 is a collection of nearly 200,000 books, taken from the library of the private torrent tracker Bibliotik.

However, recent deposition testimony from a former Meta researcher tells a different story, according to the rightsholders.

Books3 Torrenting Testimony

In a joint status report filed with Meta on Tuesday, the rightsholders say that Stephen Roller admitted during a deposition last week that he torrented Books3 and knowingly distributed it. Roller worked at Meta between 2017 and 2023, and the download took place during that period, they say.

Roller didn’t recall exactly when he acquired the dataset, the plaintiffs note. He did acknowledge that Books3 was created in 2020, and that he didn’t work for any other company while at Meta.

This is relevant, as the court ruled last year that training Llama on books was fair use, leaving Meta’s BitTorrent downloads as the main open issue in the authors’ case. Earlier this month, a judge ordered Meta to name the employees who approved torrenting from shadow libraries.

Meta has acknowledged using Books3 before. In early 2024, it admitted that it used portions of the dataset to train its Llama 1 and Llama 2 models. That admission didn’t say how Meta obtained the dataset.

Roller also testified that Meta had copies of Books3 by the time he left its AI research group FAIR, the plaintiffs write. He also named two research scientists who, they say, likely acquired their own copies.

Roller no longer has his own copy. According to the plaintiffs, he deleted it about a year ago, possibly after he was subpoenaed for the second time. He did so “[d]ue to all this litigation,” as “it seem[ed] contentious to have copies of The Pile [which includes Books3].”

The claim that Meta had multiple copies, at least one of them torrented, was news to the plaintiffs, they write. They plan to ask Meta how many copies of Books3 it acquired and how, and will ask the court to step in if that fails.

Meta: Could Have Been for Himself

Meta sees things differently. The company notes that the status report is the first time the rightsholders raised these concerns, and the tech giant argues that Roller’s deposition doesn’t support them.

“Mr. Roller testified that he did not know when he downloaded a copy of the ‘The Pile’ via torrent, and did not testify that his download of the ‘The Pile’ was for Meta or at Meta, noting it could have been for himself or for another employer,” Meta writes.

According to Meta, Roller also said that he didn’t know whether more than one copy was downloaded, or whether the two researchers he mentioned acquired Books3. He left Meta in January 2023 and has since worked for three other companies working on AI.

The deleted copy was stored on Roller’s personal computer, Meta adds. He removed it more than two years after leaving the company because he “didn’t need it, so [he’d] rather not have it.”

A (Pirated) Book Club

Books3 is not the only pirated material that comes up in the status report. The plaintiffs also suggest that pirated books may have been used at Meta for things other than AI training.

They want Meta to produce the contents of an internal Google Drive folder titled “ML Books”. In addition, they want records of a Meta book club that may have used books from shadow libraries.

In one of the documents Meta produced, an employee shared a “pirated book” with a colleague. “i know for vellum sake this is prob very ironic,” the employee wrote. When asked whether the book was pirated, the employee replied with a link to the “ML Books” folder.

The recipient told another colleague, “bro she tryna get me fired.” He added that he “may need her to delete those messages.”

The plaintiffs see this as relevant. If Meta employees used shadow library books for a book club, that would impact Meta’s fair use defense.

However, Meta argues that this request comes too late. The plaintiffs first asked for the linked files on October 9, which was more than a month after the discovery period had closed.

As for the folder itself, Meta says it is investigating and will discuss it with the plaintiffs when it knows more.

Missing Server Logs

Roller’s copy of Books3 is not the only material the plaintiffs say is missing. Meta still hasn’t handed over all command history files from its torrenting, they note, despite court orders to do so. According to the plaintiffs, these logs show how Meta configured its torrent software and which torrent files it targeted, and thus which works.

Specifically, Meta has yet to hand over command history files from any of the servers it used during its torrenting periods, the plaintiffs say. They now ask the court to order Meta to say whether any of these files were deleted, and when.

Meta, in turn, counters that it has produced substantial quantities of logs from those servers and is still searching backups, handing over new files on a rolling basis. According to Meta, there is no reason to believe any command history files were deleted.

Entrepreneur’s case is scheduled to go to trial in the spring of 2027, with the other publishers lined up behind it, should it settle before then. Meanwhile, the list of related cases keeps growing. This month, publishers including Elsevier, Hachette and Macmillan, as well as more authors, joined the queue.

—

A copy of the joint case management statement, filed at the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, is available here (pdf).

entry.title: Casio Watches of the 1980s
What is a light-day? The milestone Voyager 1 is closing in on
entry.content:
The Voyager 1 spacecraft, traveling for nearly 50 years, will soon cross a mile marker reached by no other human-made object — one light-day away from Earth. That’s the distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours, equaling about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), a point that Voyager 1 will reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST.

Voyager 1 to Reach One Light-Day

NOV 18, 2026, 5:16AM EST

Its twin spacecraft, Voyager 2, took a different path through the solar system after they launched in 1977, in order to visit Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 2 is on pace to be one light-day away from Earth in nine more years, in November 2035.

Why measure with light?

Nothing in the universe travels faster than light. Moving through space about 186,000 miles every second, it crosses enormous distances in a given time period, whether it’s a second, a day, or a year. This is true for any type of electromagnetic radiation, including visible light, microwaves, radio waves, gamma rays, X-rays, or infrared. A light-day is the distance that light will travel in 24 hours, or 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers).

To put this mileage into perspective, consider some other light-distances:

The Moon is 238,855 miles (384,400 kilometers) from Earth, on average. The astronauts on the Artemis II mission took about three days to get there, but light can traverse that distance in 1.3 seconds. Sunlight takes about eight minutes and 20 seconds to travel the 93 million miles from the Sun to Earth (about 150 million kilometers), meaning our nearest star is about 8.3 light-minutes away. The distance between Earth and Mars changes as they orbit the Sun, and it can take anywhere from three minutes to 22 minutes for light to travel between the two planets. Same for a radio transmission, either to or from a spacecraft at Mars. Neptune, the most distant planet in our solar system, with an average distance from Earth of about 2.8 billion miles (4.5 billion kilometers), is four light-hours and 10 light-minutes away. It took Voyager 2, traveling about 35,000 miles per hour, 12 years to reach Neptune.

That’s why light-year — how far light can travel in a year — is used to measure and convey the vastness of space. It’s about 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers). The closest neighboring solar system to our own, the star Proxima Centauri and its one or more planets, is about 4.24 light-years away (or, about 24.95 trillion miles, or 40.15 trillion kilometers). And the next-closest galaxy to our own Milky Way, the Andromeda galaxy, is about 2.5 million light-years away.

Where is Voyager 1 going?

Voyager 1 is headed in the direction of a star more than 17 light-years away from Earth called AC +79 3888, also known as Gliese 445. It’s an obscure star now in the constellation Ursa Minor (the Little Bear or Little Dipper), and Voyager 1 is expected to pass within about 1.7 light-years of it — in 40,000 years. Even though the spacecraft, in flight since 1977, is cruising at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) through the vacuum of space, that’s a relative crawl compared to the speed of light.

When Voyager 1 makes its mark Nov. 18, the spacecraft will have taken 49 years, two months, and 11 days to have traveled one light-day beyond Earth — a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating.

entry.title: Enlightenment 0.28 Released with Many Improvements
entry.content:
Enlightenment 0.28 Released With Many Improvements

Enlightenment 0.27 released at the beginning of 2025 and since then there's been no major feature update, falling off their roughly 12 month release cadence. But out this Halloween is Enlightenment 0.28 now with the better part of two years worth of changes. Carsten Haitzler released Enlightenment 0.28 today and it comes with initial NetBSD operating system support, a NetworkManager module for wired and wireless networking management along with VPNs, and various other network integration improvements. Enlightenment 0.28 also comes with native PipeWire mixer support while still retaining support for PulseAudio. There is also a variety of other audio-related enhancements to this Enlightenment update.Some of the other changes include new window actions, improved client side decoration handling, improved display mode sorting, improved backlight filtering, improved window siwtching, and a wide variety of fixes and code cleanups. On the low-level side is also improved pixmap handling, X connection recovery, and nested Wayland compositor shutdown. Enlightenment 0.28 continues to boast both X11 and Wayland support. Downloads and more details on this Enlightenment 0.28 release via Enlightenment.org.
